the-elephant-who-says-pehle-aap: A warning before boarding. Uttar Pradesh has more people than Brazil and more history than most continents. It contains the last flat edge of the Himalayan foothills, the Ganga’s longest stretch, the Bundelkhand plateau, a slice of Delhi’s suburbs and some of the poorest villages in Asia. Every generalisation below has a district, a caste or a mohalla that contradicts it. I have tried to stick to what I could check, and where I could not, I say so. But this one is also personal, and on the personal parts I am, by definition, an unreliable witness. Read it the way you would listen to an uncle on a charpai after dinner: with affection, with patience, and with the pinch of salt he would never admit you need. When someone in Geneva asks where in India I am from, I say “Lucknow, about eight hours by train from Delhi.” It is a tidy answer, and it is true, but it is not the whole answer. It leaves out the other half of me, which belongs further east, in Purvanchal. Most Europeans have heard of neither, and simply nod. Indians have heard of both, and there is a small pause after I say it. It is the pause of a person placing me — capital or countryside, Nawabs or strongmen — and deciding whether to be polite about it. I have learned to enjoy that pause. It contains most of what this essay is about. In it are the Ganga and the Gomti, the ghats of Varanasi and the imambaras of Lucknow, Kabir and Tulsidas, Premchand and Mir, Nehru’s Allahabad and eight men shot at a tehsil office in Ghazipur in 1942. In it too are the headlines: the riots, the encounters, the gangsters who became legislators and the legislators who behaved like gangsters, the young men from Ballia and Gorakhpur sleeping on railway platforms in Mumbai. The pause is a whole state trying to fit into a second. My own version of the state comes in three parts. My family belongs to Jahurabad, a village in Ghazipur district, on the eastern edge of UP where it shades into Bihar and the Ganga bends towards Bengal. I grew up in Lucknow, the capital, three hundred-odd kilometres to the west, in a city that says pehle aap, after you, and, the cynics will tell you, means it about half the time. They have not met the good people of Lucknow, for whom it means it all the time, and who will go to extraordinary lengths to make it so. And between the two sat Varanasi, close enough to the village to be the big city of every childhood trip, and the place where, whether you believe any of it or not, you learn that people in UP take death more seriously than almost anyone on earth. Threaded through all three is Rasra, in Ballia district, my mother’s hometown: the nanihaal, the mother’s home, where the rules were softer and the food more generous. Mau, Ballia and Azamgarh were the relatives’ towns, the wedding towns, the towns where someone always knew someone. The overnight train east out of Lucknow’s Charbagh station was where the two halves of my life met. The Lucknow half boarded in pressed clothes and said aap to strangers. Somewhere after midnight the dialect in the compartment changed, aap became tum and then tohar, the tea got sweeter, and by the time the train was deep in Purvanchal the man in the next berth was telling you, without being asked, which of the local strongmen he knew personally. That journey, I have come to think, is Uttar Pradesh in miniature: a courtesy at one end, a swagger at the other, and in between a very long night full of people with opinions. This essay is an attempt to explain the state that sits in that pause: where it came from, what it has given India, what it has done to itself, and what it did to me. Plate 1 Written over like an old manuscript: Lucknow’s gate, Kashi’s fires, Ghazipur’s poppies and the trains that carried everyone away. The elephant carries all of it. A country pretending to be a state Start with the number, because in UP everything starts with the number. The last census, in 2011, counted 199,812,341 people in Uttar Pradesh. There has been no count since; the next census, delayed by the pandemic and then by politics, now has its reference date in March 2027. The government’s own projection puts the state at about 244 million this October. That is roughly the population of Nigeria, the sixth most populous country on earth, and more than any country in Europe, South America or Africa. If UP were independent, it would sit between Pakistan and Brazil in the world’s table, with a seat at the UN and, presumably, a very loud delegation. It is also India’s fourth-largest state by area, and it touches nine other states and Delhi, more neighbours than any other state has. Eighty of the 543 members of the Lok Sabha are elected from it; the next largest, Maharashtra, sends forty-eight. The state assembly has 403 seats. On polling day, UP holds more voters than most countries hold people. The state is younger than its size suggests. The British built it by accretion: the territories they took from the Mughals and the Marathas became the North-Western Provinces in 1836; the kingdom of Awadh, which they annexed in 1856, was bolted on in 1877; the whole was renamed the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh in 1902. On 24 January 1950, two days before India became a republic, it became Uttar Pradesh, the “northern province”, keeping its initials, which is the sort of economy UP appreciates. In November 2000 its hill districts left to form Uttaranchal, now Uttarakhand, and the plains, which had always held most of the people, carried on. Why so many people? There are three answers, and they operate on very different clocks. The oldest is the soil. UP is mostly the middle Ganga plain, a trough filled over millions of years with Himalayan silt, flat, fertile and fed by rivers that do not dry up in summer because they are fed by snow. It is some of the best farmland on the planet, and people have been farming it intensively for about three thousand years. Dense farmland supports dense villages, and the plain has been one of the most crowded places on earth for as long as anyone has been counting. At the first all-India census in 1901, the territory that is now UP already held about 47 million people, close to a fifth of everyone in what is now India. The second is a slow demographic transition. Across India, falling death rates were followed, a generation or two later, by falling birth rates. In the south, where women were more educated and married later, the second fall came early. In UP it came late. In the National Family Health Survey of 1992–93 the average woman in UP could expect to have about 4.8 children. By 2019–21 it was 2.4, still above the national 2.0 and the replacement level of 2.1, but falling fast. The gap is closing; it has not closed. A population that was already the largest kept growing faster for longer, and the momentum of all those young people having children of their own will carry it upward for another decade or two. The third is a political choice. When India redrew its internal map along linguistic lines in the 1950s, UP was the obvious candidate for division and was not divided. In 1955 the historian K. M. Panikkar, a member of the States Reorganisation Commission, wrote a dissenting note arguing that a single state this large would unbalance the federation, and proposed carving a new state out of its western districts. He was overruled. In 2011 the UP assembly, under Mayawati, passed a resolution to split the state into four: Purvanchal in the east, Bundelkhand in the south, Awadh Pradesh in the middle and Paschim Pradesh in the west. The resolution went to Delhi and has stayed there. Everyone who governs UP discovers, sooner or later, that there is a great deal of power in being the elephant. That power is about to be tested. Parliamentary seats have been frozen since 1976 on the basis of the 1971 census, precisely so that states that controlled their populations would not be punished for it. The freeze lifts after the first census taken after 2026. If seats are redistributed by population, UP’s share of the Lok Sabha rises and the south’s falls, and the argument over whether that is democracy or a penalty for success is one of the defining fights of the coming decade. Somewhere in that argument is the whole paradox of UP: the same numbers that make it poor per head make it powerful in total. The same numbers that make UP poor per head make it powerful in total. The oldest valley There is a stone pillar inside the fort at Prayagraj, the city that most of my family still calls Allahabad, and it is the best single object I know for explaining Uttar Pradesh. It was raised in the third century BCE, probably by Ashoka, and carries his edicts. Six hundred years later a court poet named Harisena carved, on the same polished sandstone, a long praise-poem for the Gupta emperor Samudragupta, listing the kings he had conquered. Around 1605 the Mughal emperor Jahangir added his own genealogy, in Persian. In between, over the centuries, pilgrims and travellers scratched their names on it. Buddhist dharma, Sanskrit imperial boasting, Persian dynastic pride and graffiti: four civilisations, one stone, none of them bothering to erase the others. That is the state’s history in a sentence. It is not a story of one culture replacing another. It is a palimpsest, written over again and again, with everything still faintly legible underneath. Plate 2 Ashoka’s Brahmi above, a later hand’s Nagari below. The stone kept every one of them. Epics and republics The earliest layer is a mixture of memory and myth. The Ramayana’s Ayodhya, capital of the kingdom of Kosala, is on the Saryu in central UP; Krishna’s Mathura and Vrindavan are on the Yamuna in the west; the Mahabharata’s Hastinapur is near Meerut. How much of the epics happened is a question for archaeologists and believers, who rarely agree. What is certain is that by the sixth century BCE the plain was divided among the mahajanapadas, the great kingdoms and republics of early India, and that several of the most important of them — Kashi, Kosala, Vatsa, Panchala, Surasena and the Malla republic — lay inside what is now Uttar Pradesh. Into that world came a prince from the Shakya clan, on the Nepal border, who left home, found what he was looking for under a tree in Bihar and walked back west to explain it. Around 528 BCE, in a deer park at Sarnath, a few kilometres outside Varanasi, the Buddha gave his first sermon to five former companions. He spent more rainy seasons at Shravasti, in the grove of Jetavana, than anywhere else, and he died at Kushinagar, near Gorakhpur. Three of the four holiest places of Buddhism are in UP. Two and a half centuries later Ashoka raised a pillar at Sarnath topped by four lions facing the four directions; since 1950 that lion capital has been the emblem of the Republic of India, stamped on every rupee note and every passport. India, officially, looks at the world through a Buddhist monument in Varanasi district. The Jains claim the same ground: Parshvanath, the twenty-third tirthankara, is said to have been born in Varanasi, and the tradition places the births of several earlier ones in Ayodhya. Sarnath Sarnath deserves more than a sentence, because it is the most layered small place I know. The Buddha’s first sermon there, to five ascetics who had abandoned him as a backslider, is remembered as Dhammacakkappavattana, the setting in motion of the wheel of the teaching: the four noble truths and the middle way between indulgence and self-torture. On that spot a whole monastic city grew. Ashoka raised his pillar in the third century BCE; the Guptas built the great Dhamek stupa, whose solid brick-and-stone drum, around the fifth or sixth century CE, still stands more than forty metres high; and when Xuanzang came in the seventh century he counted, by his own account, some fifteen hundred monks. Then, at the end of the twelfth century, in the wars that brought the Ganga plain under the Delhi Sultanate, the monasteries were sacked and abandoned, and Buddhism, which had been born on this plain, all but disappeared from it for seven hundred years. What happened next is the palimpsest again. In 1588, under Akbar, a Mughal noble built an octagonal brick tower on top of an old Buddhist mound nearby, the Chaukhandi stupa, to mark the spot where Akbar’s father Humayun had once rested; a Mughal monument on a Buddhist ruin, commemorating an emperor’s nap. In 1835 the British archaeologist Alexander Cunningham began digging the site, and in 1904–05 the engineer F. O. Oertel uncovered, broken but magnificent, the lion capital that had crowned Ashoka’s pillar. When the Constituent Assembly chose the symbols of the new republic in 1947 and 1950, it took two things from that single object found in the dirt outside Varanasi: the four lions became the state emblem, and the wheel carved on the capital’s base, the wheel of the dharma first set turning at Sarnath, became the chakra at the centre of the national flag. Every time India flies its flag, it is quoting a sermon given in a deer park in Varanasi district. The revival came from abroad. The Sri Lankan Buddhist reformer Anagarika Dharmapala campaigned for decades to restore the Buddhist holy places, and in 1931 his Maha Bodhi Society opened a new temple at Sarnath, the Mulagandha Kuti Vihara, its walls painted by a Japanese artist, Kosetsu Nosu. Thailand, Japan, China, Myanmar, Tibet and Sri Lanka have since built temples there, so that a walk through the village is a small tour of Buddhist Asia. And the Tibetans came, in a way that ties Sarnath to the twentieth century’s great exile. When the fourteenth Dalai Lama fled Tibet in March 1959, his first home in India was not Dharamsala but Mussoorie, a hill station that was then part of Uttar Pradesh; he lived there, at Birla House, for a year, until April 1960, before moving to Dharamsala in Himachal. It was in Mussoorie, in UP, that the Tibetan government-in-exile first took shape. In 1967, with the support of Jawaharlal Nehru’s government, a Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies was founded at Sarnath to preserve the scholarship of the monasteries that had been lost; it is now the Central University of Tibetan Studies, and one of its long-serving directors, Samdhong Rinpoche, went on to become the elected prime minister of the Tibetans in exile. The Dalai Lama has returned to Sarnath many times to teach. There is something right about it: the tradition that left this plain eight hundred years ago came back, in exile, to the deer park where it began. I first went to Sarnath as a child, with my parents, and remember mostly the heat and the ice cream. I did not understand then that I was standing at the source of the wheel on my own flag. I went back in 2025, as an adult, and it was only then that the place landed: that a sermon given to five ascetics in a deer park is what India chose to put on its flag and its passport, and that the four lions I had seen on every rupee note of my life had been dug out of the ground a short walk away. Empires on the Ganga The Kushans made Mathura, around the first and second centuries CE, one of the two great workshops of early Indian sculpture; some of the earliest images of the Buddha as a human figure were carved there, in the local red sandstone. The Guptas, whose age is remembered as classical India’s golden one, left their boast on the Allahabad pillar. In the seventh century Harsha ruled northern India from Kannauj, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who visited, described a rich city of monasteries and temples. Kannauj was so prized that for the next two centuries three dynasties — the Pratiharas, the Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan — fought over it in what historians call the tripartite struggle. Today Kannauj is famous mainly for perfume. Empires come and go; attar lasts. Then the plain became the prize of a new set of conquerors. Mahmud of Ghazni sacked Mathura and Kannauj in 1018. In 1194 Muhammad of Ghor defeated Jaichand of Kannauj at Chandawar, near Etawah, and the Ganga plain passed, over the following decades, into the Delhi Sultanate. For the next five and a half centuries, most of UP was ruled from Delhi or Agra, or by governors who took orders from there when it suited them. Those centuries built half of what the world now thinks of as India. The Sharqi sultans of Jaunpur, independent from 1394 to 1479, made their city such a centre of learning that it was called the Shiraz of India, and built mosques, like the Atala, whose great gateways look like temples translated into Arabic; the Atala itself stands where a temple once stood. The Mughals made Agra their capital; Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri, a red sandstone city beside the tomb of a Sufi saint, and held debates there between Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Christian scholars. Between 1632 and 1653 his grandson Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, and gave UP the one building everyone on earth recognises. The same dynasty broke things too, and it would be dishonest to leave that out. In 1669 Aurangzeb ordered the demolition of the Kashi Vishwanath temple in Varanasi, and a mosque, the Gyanvapi, was built on part of its site; the next year he did the same to the great Keshavdeva temple at Mathura. The present Vishwanath temple was built beside the mosque in 1780 by Ahilyabai Holkar, the Maratha queen of Indore. Both buildings are still standing, wall to wall, and both are still in court. The palimpsest, in UP, is not only on pillars. Awadh The part of this history I grew up inside began in 1722, when a Persian nobleman named Saadat Khan was made the Mughal governor of Awadh, the old land of Kosala. As the empire weakened, his descendants, the Nawabs, became kings in all but name. They ruled from Faizabad, near Ayodhya, until 1775, when the Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula moved the court to Lucknow, a modest town on the Gomti, and set about turning it into the most extravagant city in India. It was in Awadh that the East India Company learned how to own a country without appearing to. In 1764, at Buxar, just across the Ganga from Ghazipur district, the Company defeated the combined armies of the Nawab of Awadh, the Nawab of Bengal and the Mughal emperor. The Treaty of Allahabad that followed gave it the right to collect the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, and reduced Awadh to a buffer state that paid for the Company’s troops. For ninety years the Nawabs were allowed to spend lavishly on poetry, music, architecture and food, while the Company took more and more of their land and their revenue. In February 1856, citing misgovernment, it annexed what was left and sent the last king, Wajid Ali Shah, poet, dancer and composer, into exile in Calcutta. The British called it misgovernment. The people of Awadh called it something else, and fifteen months later they said so. Rebels, from Ballia to Allahabad The British called what happened in 1857 a mutiny. For a long time Indians called it the First War of Independence. Historians now tend to call it the rebellion or the uprising, which is less stirring and more accurate: it was many revolts at once, by soldiers, landlords, peasants, dispossessed princes and religious leaders, with different grievances and no single plan. What is not in dispute is where its heart was. It was Uttar Pradesh. The Company’s Bengal Army was recruited overwhelmingly from Awadh and the eastern districts: tall, high-caste peasant boys from villages like the ones my family comes from, known across India as purbiyas, easterners. When the army turned, it was their villages that turned with it. The first shots, in the story every Indian schoolchild learns, were fired on 29 March 1857 at Barrackpore near Calcutta by a sepoy named Mangal Pandey, who was hanged a week later. He was born in Nagwa, in Ballia district. The eastern districts have been claiming the rebellion ever since, with some justification and a good deal of volume. The uprising proper began at Meerut, in western UP, on 10 May, when sepoys freed comrades who had been jailed for refusing the new greased cartridges, shot their officers and marched on Delhi. Within weeks it had spread across the plain. At Lucknow the British garrison held out in the Residency for months against a siege led, in the name of her young son, by Begum Hazrat Mahal, one of Wajid Ali Shah’s wives, who refused every British offer of a pension and died in exile in Kathmandu. At Kanpur, Nana Sahib, the adopted heir of the last Peshwa, besieged the British entrenchment; the surrendering garrison was massacred at the river at Satichaura Ghat, and the women and children who survived were later killed at a house called the Bibighar. At Jhansi, the widowed Rani Lakshmibai rode out against the British and died fighting in 1858. And across the eastern districts the old Rajput landlord Kunwar Singh of Jagdishpur fought a guerrilla campaign into his eighties; the story in Ballia is that, wounded by a British bullet while crossing the Ganga, he cut off his own arm and offered it to the river. Kunwar Singh was about eighty in 1858. The story of the arm is told throughout the Bhojpur region, usually placing the crossing near Shivpur ghat, opposite Ballia; he reached Jagdishpur and died there within days. The details belong to tradition rather than the record. The British reprisals were at least as terrible as the massacres, and on a far larger scale. Along the Grand Trunk Road and in the villages of Awadh, suspected rebels were hanged from trees in their hundreds, sometimes without anything resembling a trial; villages were burned; Delhi and Lucknow were sacked. Awadh passed to the Crown. The purbiya peasant-soldier, the backbone of the army that had conquered India for the Company, was recategorised as unreliable, and recruitment shifted to Punjab and the hills. The east of UP, which had given the empire its army, was left to farm, to migrate and to remember. The long road to 1947 When the national movement came, it came through UP again, in forms as various as the rebellion. In 1916 the Congress and the Muslim League, meeting in Lucknow, agreed the Lucknow Pact, the high point of Hindu–Muslim political cooperation before Partition. At Anand Bhawan in Allahabad, Motilal Nehru and his son Jawaharlal turned a lawyer’s mansion into the movement’s northern headquarters. On 4 February 1922, at Chauri Chaura near Gorakhpur, a crowd of protesters set fire to a police station, killing more than twenty policemen inside; Gandhi, horrified, called off the entire Non-cooperation Movement, a decision many of his younger followers never forgave. Some of those young followers took up guns. On 9 August 1925, members of the Hindustan Republican Association stopped a train at Kakori, just outside Lucknow, and took the government cash it was carrying. Four of them were hanged in December 1927. Two of the four were friends from Shahjahanpur: Ram Prasad Bismil, an Arya Samaji Hindu who wrote poetry in Urdu, and Ashfaqulla Khan, a Pathan Muslim who wrote it in Urdu too. Their friendship is still invoked in UP whenever someone needs proof that Hindus and Muslims once died for each other rather than because of each other. In 1921 a fifteen-year-old Sanskrit student in Varanasi, arrested during the non-cooperation protests, gave his name to the magistrate as “Azad”, free; Chandrashekhar Azad kept the name until 1931, when, surrounded by police in a park in Allahabad, he used his last bullet on himself rather than be taken. A month later, in Kanpur, the editor Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi walked into a riot to rescue people from both communities and was killed by a mob. It is a UP story that he is less famous than he should be. Gandhi comes to the heartland It is easy to tell the story of the freedom movement as a series of heroic moments. In UP, it is more useful to tell it as a series of rooms: the lecture hall, the village meeting, the college founded in a hurry, the tent at a Congress session where two strangers happened to meet. Gandhi walked into several of those rooms, and in UP several of them changed him as much as he changed them. The first was in Varanasi. In February 1916, at the ceremonies for the founding of the Banaras Hindu University, a recently returned lawyer from South Africa, still barely known outside Gujarat, stood before an audience glittering with maharajas in their jewels and told them, in effect, that India would not be free while its princes wore its wealth on their bodies and its students were taught in a foreign language. The meeting broke up in uproar. It was the first time most of north India’s elite had heard him, and many of them never forgot it. The second was a tent. At the Congress session in Lucknow in December 1916, the same session that produced the Lucknow Pact, a peasant from Champaran in Bihar named Rajkumar Shukla followed Gandhi around until he agreed to come and see the indigo planters’ abuses for himself. Champaran, Gandhi’s first great satyagraha in India, began in a conversation in Lucknow. The third was the village. In 1920, in Pratapgarh and Rae Bareli, peasants organised by a wandering ascetic and Ramcharitmanas-reciter known as Baba Ramchandra formed the Awadh Kisan Sabha to resist the illegal levies and evictions of the taluqdars. A young barrister from Allahabad, Jawaharlal Nehru, went to see them that June, and later wrote that the experience of those crowded, hungry, hopeful villages was the moment he discovered India. The following year, in the districts of Hardoi and Bahraich, the Eka movement, led by a Pasi peasant named Madari Pasi, went further than the Congress wanted, and was put down. The Congress was learning, in UP, that the masses it had summoned did not always wait for instructions. The fourth was the college founded in a hurry. When Gandhi and the Khilafat leaders called for students to leave government-aided institutions in 1920, nationalist teachers and students at Aligarh walked out and founded, on 29 October 1920, a new national Muslim university, the Jamia Millia Islamia; it moved to Delhi in 1925, and its chancellor from 1928 was Mukhtar Ahmed Ansari, the grandfather of the man whose funeral Ghazipur watched in 2024. The Khilafat movement’s leaders, the Ali brothers, were from Rampur. In February 1921 Gandhi inaugurated the Kashi Vidyapith in Varanasi, another national university, and one of its early graduates, a small, quiet young man from Mughalsarai, took from it the degree title Shastri, which he kept as his name. Lal Bahadur Shastri became prime minister in 1964. The fifth room was the one the historian Shahid Amin made famous. Gandhi visited Gorakhpur on 8 February 1921, and in the months that followed, as Amin showed in a celebrated essay, the villages of the district filled with stories of the Mahatma’s miraculous powers: of people who doubted him punished, of wells that filled at his name, of cows restored. The peasants of eastern UP, in other words, took Gandhi and made him into something he had never claimed to be, a saint with the power to overturn the local order. A year later, at Chauri Chaura in the same district, a crowd shouting his name burned a police station with the policemen inside. Gandhi’s horrified withdrawal of the whole national movement was, in part, a recognition that in the east his name had escaped his control. After the trial, 172 people were sentenced to death; Madan Mohan Malaviya argued the appeals, and the sentence was carried out on nineteen. The rooms kept coming. In December 1925 the Congress met in Kanpur and was presided over, for the first time, by an Indian woman, Sarojini Naidu. On 30 November 1928, when the all-white Simon Commission arrived in Lucknow to consider India’s constitutional future without a single Indian member, the protest outside was charged by mounted police; Jawaharlal Nehru was beaten, and Govind Ballabh Pant, shielding him, took blows that are said to have troubled him for the rest of his life. In 1929 Gandhi toured the province to raise money for khadi, the hand-spun, hand-woven cloth that he made the uniform of the movement, and in a province full of weavers the spinning wheel was not only a symbol. In 1930, during the salt satyagraha, the Congress in UP went further than anywhere else, calling on peasants to withhold rent and revenue altogether. That December, at the Muslim League’s session in Allahabad, the poet Muhammad Iqbal proposed, for the first time from such a platform, a consolidated Muslim state in north-western India. The idea that became Pakistan was first spoken aloud a few streets from Anand Bhawan. In April 1936 Lucknow held two meetings in the same week that between them describe the century. The Congress met under Nehru, who used his presidential address to argue for socialism. And a few days earlier, in the same city, a group of young writers held the founding conference of the All-India Progressive Writers’ Association, and asked Premchand, then in the last months of his life, to preside. In his address he told them that literature would have to change its idea of beauty, and find it in the labourer, the peasant and the poor. Hindi and Urdu literature for the next forty years, from Faiz to Kaifi Azmi to the film songs of Sahir, flowed from that room. The last room, before 1942, was the ministry. In 1937 the Congress won the provincial elections and Govind Ballabh Pant became premier of the United Provinces. The Muslim League, which had done badly, hoped for places in the government and was refused unless it merged into the Congress. Historians still argue about how much that refusal in Lucknow, as much as anything Jinnah did in Bombay, pushed the League towards the demand for a separate country. UP’s rooms, in other words, produced both the partnership of 1916 and the rupture of 1947. The province that met in the same tent also taught its two communities to meet in separate ones. 1942 In August 1942, when the Congress leaders were arrested at the start of the Quit India movement, the eastern districts went further than anywhere else in India. In Ballia, crowds freed prisoners and, for a few days, ran their own government under a local leader, Chittu Pandey; the district has called itself Baghi Ballia, rebel Ballia, ever since. In Ghazipur, on 18 August, a group led by a young doctor named Shivpujan Rai marched from the village of Sherpur to the tehsil office at Mohammadabad to raise the tricolour. The tehsildar opened fire and eight of them were killed. For a few days afterwards, much of Ghazipur district was effectively in the hands of its own people. The British then took their revenge, as they had in 1857, on the villages. I grew up with those names the way children elsewhere grow up with football teams. They were on school walls and in the speeches of every visiting politician. What I did not learn at school, and learned much later, is that the same decade produced the other half of UP’s story. The Aligarh Muslim University, founded as a college by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan in 1875 to give Muslims a modern education, became by the 1940s what Jinnah is said to have called the arsenal of Muslim India The remark about Aligarh as the arsenal of Muslim India is widely attributed to Jinnah, but the exact wording and occasion vary between sources., and in the 1946 elections Muslim voters in UP backed the League overwhelmingly. When Partition came, the violence in UP was far less than in Punjab and Bengal, but a large part of its Muslim professional class, its lawyers, civil servants and poets, left for Karachi, where their descendants still speak an Urdu that sounds like Lucknow and are still called muhajirs, migrants. The state that had done the most to hold India’s two great communities together also did a great deal to separate them. Both are true, and UP has never quite decided which to remember. Lucknow, or the art of saying after you Every Lucknowi knows the joke, and every Lucknowi tells it as though it had never been told before. Two gentlemen arrive on the platform at Charbagh as the train pulls in. Pehle aap, says one, gesturing towards the door. Nahin, pehle aap, insists the other. They are still saying it, with increasing elegance, as the train leaves without them. The joke is about excess, and Lucknow was built on excess. Asaf-ud-Daula, the Nawab who moved the court here in 1775, was so famously generous that the city still repeats a rhyme about him: jisko na de Maula, usko de Asaf-ud-Daula, whoever God neglects to provide for, Asaf-ud-Daula will. In 1784, during a famine, he began building the Bara Imambara, a vast Shia congregation hall with one of the largest vaulted halls in the world built without beams, as a relief works; the story in the old city, impossible to verify and too good to leave out, is that the respectable poor, too proud to be seen labouring, were employed at night to pull down part of what had been built by day, so that the work, and the wages, would last. The story of the Bara Imambara’s night-time demolitions is told all over old Lucknow and in most guidebooks. I have not found a contemporary source for it, and it may be an embroidery on the well-documented fact that the building was begun as a famine relief works in 1784. Whether or not it is true, it tells you what Lucknow thinks dignity is: something so important that you build a building around it. Plate 3 A city that built a gateway just to be walked through politely. Tehzeeb The word Lucknow uses for itself is tehzeeb, which dictionaries translate as culture, or refinement, and which in practice means a whole grammar of manners. You greet people with adab, a slight bow with the hand raised towards the forehead, rather than namaste or salaam, a greeting that belongs to no religion and so to everyone. You say aap to the rickshaw puller. You say hum, we, instead of main, I, when you speak of yourself, which to outsiders sounds either royal or absurd and to Lucknowis sounds simply correct: the self, in polite company, should not stand alone. You refuse food twice before accepting. You deliver an insult so courteously that the recipient thanks you for it and only works it out on the way home. Two other words sit beside it. Nazakat is delicacy: of movement, of speech, of embroidery, of a kebab so soft it was supposedly invented for a toothless Nawab. Nafasat is refinement of taste. Together they describe a culture that valued the manner of doing a thing at least as much as the thing, and that is how you get the Lucknow gharana of kathak, where a dancer can tell an entire story with the flick of an eyebrow; the thumri, a light-classical song form polished at Wajid Ali Shah’s court; chikankari, white-on-white embroidery so fine it is sometimes described as shadow work; and the city’s food, cooked slowly in sealed pots, dum pukht, until the flavour has nowhere to go but inwards. The last king of Awadh left Lucknow in 1856 for exile in Calcutta, and the song most associated with him, sung for more than a century and a half since by everyone from courtesans to K. L. Saigal, is a bride’s farewell to her father’s house: बाबुल मोरा नैहर छूटो ही जाय bābul morā naihar chhūṭo hī jāy Father, my father’s house is slipping away from me. Whether Wajid Ali Shah wrote it about his own exile, as the city likes to believe, or whether it was an older song he made famous, nobody can now say for certain. Lucknow has always preferred the better story. Babul mora is almost universally attributed to Wajid Ali Shah; some musicologists think he may have set or reworked an older folk song. A city of poets, and of arguments about poetry Lucknow’s Urdu poetry developed as a rival to Delhi’s. When Delhi was sacked, first by Nadir Shah in 1739 and then repeatedly by everyone else, its poets drifted east to the Nawabs’ court, and the greatest of them, Mir Taqi Mir, arrived in 1782, disliked almost everything about the place, said so in verse, and stayed until he died in 1810. The Lucknow school came to be known for ornament, wordplay and sensuous detail, the Delhi school for inwardness; they insulted each other for a century. The city’s greatest poetic achievement, though, was the marsiya, the elegy for the martyrs of Karbala, which Mir Anis and Mirza Dabeer turned in the nineteenth century into something close to an Urdu epic. The Nawabs were Shia, and Muharram in Lucknow, the processions, the tazias, the recitations, remains one of the city’s defining sights, attended, as it always has been, by a good many Hindus. In 1899 Mirza Hadi Ruswa published Umrao Jaan Ada, the story of a girl kidnapped and sold to a Lucknow courtesan’s house who becomes its most celebrated poet and dancer; it is often called the first Urdu novel, and it is still the book through which much of India imagines the old city. Premchand’s short story Shatranj ke Khiladi, the chess players, published in 1924 and filmed by Satyajit Ray in 1977, gave the other image: two noblemen so absorbed in their chess that they fail to notice the British annexing their kingdom. Lucknow has never quite decided whether that story is an affectionate portrait or an indictment. It is both, which is why it lasts. What the manners hide The professor has to interrupt here, because nostalgia is the city’s main industry and someone has to audit it. Tehzeeb was, originally, a court culture, and courts rest on hierarchy. The same exquisite manners that required you to say aap to a servant also required the servant to stand while you sat. The courtesans whose poetry the city celebrates were, many of them, girls who had been trafficked into the courtesans’ houses as children. The Nawabs’ extravagance was paid for by peasants in the countryside of Awadh, one of the most oppressive landlord systems in India, and the taluqdars, the great landlords the British left in place after 1857, were abolished only with the zamindari abolition of 1951. And the same Shia–Sunni devotion that produced the marsiya produced, in the twentieth century, recurring sectarian clashes over rival public recitations, serious enough that processions were banned for decades. Lucknow’s courtesy has always had a back entrance. The modern city has added its own layers. It is a Hindi city now as much as an Urdu one: Amritlal Nagar wrote here, and Yashpal, and Srilal Shukla, whose Raag Darbari, set in a village a few hours away, is still the best book ever written about how power works in UP. It is a city of universities and research institutes, of the Central Drug Research Institute and a medical college founded in 1911, of La Martiniere, built with a French adventurer’s fortune, and Isabella Thoburn, one of the first colleges for women in Asia. It is a city of new ring roads and a metro and, in Gomti Nagar, of the vast pink-stone parks Mayawati built as memorials to Dalit leaders, lined with rows of stone elephants, her party’s symbol. When I was a teenager we laughed at the elephants. I laugh less now. They are, among other things, the first public monuments in the city’s history built to honour people whom the old tehzeeb would have kept standing at the door. What Lucknow gave me, and I will come back to this, was the belief that the way you say a thing is part of what you are saying. I still think that is true. I also think a city that believes it so completely should be the first to ask who was doing the serving while everyone else was being polite. Kashi, where they come to die Mark Twain, who was not easily impressed by anything holy, visited Varanasi in 1896 and wrote that it was older than history, older than tradition, older even than legend, and looked twice as old as all of them put together. Archaeologists would quibble; there has been continuous settlement on the site for about three thousand years, which makes it one of the oldest living cities on earth but not older than legend. Anyone who has stood on the ghats at dawn will forgive Twain the exaggeration. Varanasi has three names and uses all of them. Varanasi, the official one, is taken from the two small rivers, the Varuna and the Assi, between which it lies. Banaras is the one most people in UP actually say. Kashi, the oldest, means the city of light, and it is the one used by people who have come to the city for the reason most pilgrims have always come: to die in it. The belief is simple and very old. Shiva, who is said to have made Kashi his home, whispers into the ear of anyone who dies within the city the mantra that frees them from the cycle of rebirth. To die in Kashi is to attain moksha, liberation. So people come, old and ill, to wait. Since 1958 a charitable house near the river, the Kashi Labh Mukti Bhawan, has given the dying a room for up to about two weeks; if death has not come by then, they are gently asked to go home and try again another time. On the burning ghats at Manikarnika and Harishchandra, the pyres have not gone out, the city says, in thousands of years. The wood is weighed on scales, priced by the kilo. The Doms, the community who have tended the fires for centuries, and who were long subjected to untouchability by the same religion whose most sacred rite they perform, keep the flame. The first time I watched a body burn at Manikarnika I was a child, and I remember being told not to be frightened because the man was lucky. I did not understand then that this was the most important thing anyone had told me about the city. Varanasi does not hide death. It weighs it, prices it, argues over it, sings about it and cooks lunch beside it. It is the only place I know where the question every other city is organised to avoid is the city’s main business. Plate 4 The only city I know whose main business is the question every other city avoids. The poets of the ghats For a city devoted to one god, Varanasi has produced an astonishing number of people who argued with him. Kabir was a weaver, born into a Muslim weaving family in the fifteenth century, and the legend is that he was found as a baby by a pond at Lahartara, on the edge of the city. He mocked the Brahmin and the mullah with equal enthusiasm, the idol and the mosque, the pilgrimage and the fast, and insisted that God was neither in Kashi nor in Kaaba but inside the person looking for him. His couplets, the dohe, are still the most quoted verses in north India, recited by schoolchildren and politicians who would have infuriated him. At the end of his life, the story goes, he left Kashi for Maghar, a town near Gorakhpur where it was believed that anyone who died would be reborn as a donkey, precisely to show that the place of death meant nothing. When he died, his Hindu and Muslim followers quarrelled over whether to cremate or bury him; when they lifted the shroud, the legend says, they found only flowers, which they divided. In Maghar today a Hindu samadhi and a Muslim tomb stand side by side. Ravidas, a leatherworker from a village just outside the city, from one of the communities the caste order branded as polluting, sang of a city without sorrow, Begampura, where there would be no tax, no fear and no second-class citizens. Forty of his hymns are in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, and his birthplace at Seer Govardhanpur is now a place of pilgrimage for millions of Dalits. In the sixteenth century Tulsidas, living by the Assi ghat, wrote the Ramcharitmanas, the Ramayana retold in Awadhi, the language of ordinary people rather than Sanskrit, and in doing so made the story of Ram the common property of the entire Hindi-speaking world; it is still read aloud, in full, in homes and temples across north India. The Sanskrit pandits of Kashi, the story goes, were furious that the sacred story had been put into the vernacular. They lost. There is an older story too, the one I like best. Adi Shankaracharya, the eighth-century philosopher of non-dualism, was walking to the river in Kashi when a man of the community the old texts called chandala, pushed to the very bottom of the caste order, crossed his path, and Shankara’s disciples told the man to get out of the way. The chandala asked whether it was his body that should move aside, or his self, and if the self, how the self of one man could be different from the self of another, when Shankara himself taught that they were one. Shankara, the story says, bowed to him, and wrote five verses, the Manisha Panchakam, declaring that whoever had realised that truth was his teacher, whatever his birth. The greatest intellectual of Hindu philosophy, corrected about caste by a man his own disciples had ordered out of the way, on the way to the Ganga, in Kashi. The city has been telling that story for twelve centuries and has not always listened to it. Music, silk and the Malaviya problem Varanasi is also the city of Bismillah Khan, a devout Shia Muslim who played the shehnai every morning at a temple on the Ganga, and who, the story in the city goes, turned down an invitation to settle in America because nobody could bring him the Ganga; The Bismillah Khan anecdote is widely reported in many versions, with different people doing the inviting. What is certain is that he lived in Varanasi until his death in 2006. of Ravi Shankar, born here in 1920; of the singers Siddheshwari Devi and Girija Devi, the queens of thumri; of the tabla of Kishan Maharaj. It is the city of the Banarasi silk sari, woven for centuries on handlooms mostly by Muslim weaving families, the Ansaris, for Hindu brides, a trade the powerloom and the cheap import have been slowly killing. It is also a city of institutions. In 1898 Annie Besant, the theosophist, founded the Central Hindu College here; in 1916 Madan Mohan Malaviya, a lawyer and Congress leader, turned it into the Banaras Hindu University, one of the largest residential universities in Asia, where Jayant Narlikar grew up on the campus and the country’s engineers have been trained for a century. Malaviya was a liberal nationalist who presided over the Congress four times and a founder of the Hindu Mahasabha; he opposed untouchability and defended the old orthodoxy in the same career. He is a very Varanasi figure: reformer and conservative at once, and quite sure there is no contradiction. In December 2021 the government opened the Kashi Vishwanath corridor, a broad stone passage from the river to the temple, cutting through lanes and demolishing hundreds of old houses and dozens of small shrines along the way. Pilgrims love it; the numbers have multiplied. Old Banarasis argue about it, the way they argue about everything. The Gyanvapi mosque still stands beside the temple, and the lawsuits over it still stand beside the mosque. What Kashi gave me is harder to say than what Lucknow gave me. It was not a religion; I have been arguing with religion in these pages for years, and I am not about to stop. It was something closer to a posture: the idea that the most serious questions are asked out loud, on a riverbank, with other people’s funerals going on beside you and a boy selling tea through the smoke. Kabir, Ravidas, Tulsidas and the chandala who corrected Shankara all argued about God in the same few kilometres of river. None of them thought the argument was disrespectful. In Kashi, the argument is the prayer. In Kashi, the argument is the prayer. Purab: poppies, soldiers and ships The east of Uttar Pradesh is called Purvanchal by the government and purab, simply the east, by everyone else. Ghazipur, Ballia, Mau, Azamgarh, Jaunpur, Varanasi, Gorakhpur, Deoria: a flat, crowded, flood-prone country of mango orchards, sugarcane, brick kilns and the Ganga and the Ghaghra, closer in speech and food and temper to western Bihar than to western UP. It is the poorest and most densely populated part of an already poor and crowded state. It is where I am from, in the sense in which Indians mean that question, which is not where you were born but where your people’s land is. Ghazipur Ghazipur sits on the north bank of the Ganga, about seventy kilometres downstream of Varanasi. Local tradition gives it two origins, one Hindu and one Muslim — an ancient Gadhipur, named for a legendary king, and a medieval renaming after a Muslim warrior, a ghazi — and like most such pairs of stories in UP they are told by different people, and both are probably partly true. The town’s most famous grave belongs to a man who had nothing to do with either: Charles Cornwallis, the British general who surrendered to George Washington at Yorktown, went on to be Governor-General of India, and died at Ghazipur in October 1805 while travelling upriver. His domed tomb is still there, beside the Ganga, looking faintly surprised. Ghazipur’s real contribution to world history was a flower. In 1820 the East India Company opened a factory in the town to process opium from the poppy fields of the Ganga plain, and for the rest of the century Ghazipur opium, packed into balls and shipped downriver to Calcutta, went on to Canton, paid for Britain’s tea and helped cause two wars with China. The factory still runs, under the government, making legal opium alkaloids for the pharmaceutical industry. Amitav Ghosh’s novel Sea of Poppies begins in the poppy fields near Ghazipur, with a woman named Deeti, and follows her onto a ship. The ship is the other half of the story. Between the 1830s and 1917, after the abolition of slavery in the British Empire, more than a million Indians were shipped as indentured labourers to work the sugar plantations of Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad, British Guiana, Suriname, Natal and elsewhere. They were called girmitiyas, from their mispronunciation of the “agreement” they signed, often without being able to read it. The largest single group came from the Bhojpuri-speaking districts of eastern UP and western Bihar: Ghazipur, Ballia, Azamgarh, Basti, Gonda, Arrah, Chhapra. Their descendants are the reason Bhojpuri is spoken in Port Louis and Paramaribo, the reason several prime ministers of Mauritius, Trinidad and Guyana have had names that would not surprise anyone in Ballia, and the reason the Bhojpuri folk tradition is full of bidesia songs, sung by women whose husbands have gone bides, abroad, and not come back. Every family in the east has an uncle who went to Calcutta, a great-grandfather who went to Rangoon, a rumour about someone who went to Fiji. Migration is not a recent problem in Purvanchal. It is the oldest thing the region knows how to do. The district has also given India a remarkable run of people who became something without leaving it behind. In 1890 a young Bengali monk named Narendranath Datta, not yet Swami Vivekananda, came to Ghazipur to meet a hermit called Pavhari Baba, the “air-eating” saint, who lived in an underground cell by the river and was said to eat almost nothing; Vivekananda nearly became his disciple, and held him ever after second only to Ramakrishna. The writer Rahi Masoom Raza was born in 1927 in Gangauli, a Shia village in the district, and wrote Aadha Gaon, Half a Village, about how Partition split it; he went on to write the dialogue for B. R. Chopra’s television Mahabharat, the serial that emptied India’s streets on Sunday mornings in 1988 and 1989, and never saw any contradiction in a Muslim from Ghazipur putting words into the mouth of Krishna. Nazir Hussain, born in the village of Usia and a veteran of the Indian National Army, persuaded India’s first president that his mother tongue deserved a cinema, and in 1963 made Ganga Maiyya Tohe Piyari Chadhaibo, the first Bhojpuri film. And in 1965, at Asal Uttar in Punjab, Company Quartermaster Havildar Abdul Hamid of Dhamupur, Ghazipur, destroyed several Pakistani Patton tanks with a jeep-mounted recoilless gun before he was killed, and was awarded the Param Vir Chakra; Rahi Masoom Raza wrote a book about him. Gangauli is not far from my own village, near enough that it belonged to the same small world of market towns, bus routes and relatives’ weddings. I once visited Rahi’s ancestral home in passing, the way you visit things in the east: someone in the car mentions that this is where he was from, the car stops, you stand in front of an old house for a few minutes, and then you drive on to wherever you were actually going. I did not know then how much of what I would later believe about the east was already written in Aadha Gaon: that a village can be Shia and Hindu and Bhojpuri all at once, that it can mourn Karbala in Muharram and argue about land like everyone else, and that a line drawn by lawyers in Delhi and Karachi could cut straight through it. Rahi spent his life insisting that he was a son of the Ganga and of Ghazipur, and that nobody had the right to hand him a different country. Standing in front of his house, I understood, a little late, that he had been writing about my district all along. It is one of the quiet facts of Jahurabad’s politics that in 2012 its seat in the assembly was won by a woman born in Gangauli. The district is soldier country. Gahmar, a village on the Ganga in Ghazipur, is often called the largest village in Asia, and it is said that almost every family in it has sent a son to the army, a tradition that goes back to the purbiya sepoys of the Company. The claims are the kind that villages make about themselves, and I have never seen a count I trust. Gahmar is regularly described as one of the largest villages in Asia, and its tradition of army service is real, but population figures depend on where the village is counted to end, and the proportion of families with a soldier is local pride rather than statistics. The fact underneath them is not in doubt: for two hundred years the east has exported soldiers, labourers and migrants because it could not feed all of its sons at home. Jahurabad My family’s village is in the north-east of the district, towards Ballia, and gives its name to an assembly constituency. The old records describe it as the seat of a jagir, an estate held under the Mughals and then the British by a family of Pathan landlords, and at the census of 1901 the village itself held about 1,270 people, of whom more than 550 were Muslims. I did not know this growing up. What I knew was what every child from such a place knows: the particular smell of the earth after the first rain, the hand-pump, the mango orchard where the older boys disappeared in the afternoons, the long evenings on a charpai while the men argued about land, marriages and elections, in exactly that order of seriousness. The constituency is now represented by Om Prakash Rajbhar, leader of a party built on the Rajbhar community, one of the backward classes that the old zamindari order kept at the bottom. In a hundred years, the village has gone from a Pathan landlord’s estate to a Rajbhar politician’s seat. That is a short sentence for a very long revolution. Ballia, Mau and Rasra Ballia, across the district line, is where the east keeps its pride. It gave India Mangal Pandey, Chittu Pandey’s three-day republic of 1942, and a prime minister, Chandra Shekhar, born in the village of Ibrahimpatti, a socialist who once walked four thousand kilometres across India and governed the country for seven months in 1990 and 1991. It gave Hindi one of its finest critics and novelists, Hazari Prasad Dwivedi. Its people will tell you all of this within ten minutes of meeting you, and will then tell you that the rest of India has never given Ballia its due, which, to be fair, is true. Mau, to the north, was a weaving town, famous for its handloom saris and the Muslim weaving families who made them, until it became better known for its politics; it was carved out as a separate district in 1988, largely through the influence of one local politician, which is itself a very Purvanchal way for a district to be born. Rasra, in Ballia, is my mother’s town: a market town and railway stop, and for me the nanihaal, where a child from Lucknow was fed without limit, forgiven almost anything, and met at the station by uncles in a jeep that had seen better decades. Azamgarh, next door, where a good part of the extended family is scattered, gave the world the travelling scholar Rahul Sankrityayan and the poet Kaifi Azmi, and in the 2000s acquired, after a handful of its young men were accused in terror cases, a national reputation it has never deserved and never shaken off. Dabangai There is a word for the quality the east is known for, and it is not a compliment everywhere. Dabang means fearless, forceful, a little overbearing; dabangai is the habit of being so. It is the swagger of a man who says hum kaun hain, jaante ho?, do you know who I am, and expects you to. It is a lathi on the shoulder at a village wedding, a country pistol, a katta, fired into the air when the groom arrives, a dispute over a boundary ridge settled by who can bring more cousins. It is a politics of strongmen, bahubalis, which I will come to. It is the reason a certain kind of Bollywood film is always set in eastern UP or Bihar. But it is also, and this is the part outsiders miss, a code. It is loyalty to your own, the refusal to be humiliated, the obligation to stand up when someone from your village is in trouble in a city where nobody else will. It is the courage that sent Shivpujan Rai walking towards a tehsildar’s revolver with a flag in his hand, and Abdul Hamid towards a Patton tank. It is what a poor, crowded, flooded, twice-colonised country produces in people who have learned that no one is coming to help. The line between that courage and plain thuggery is thin, and the east has crossed it more often than it likes to admit. It is still a line, and I have spent a good part of my life trying to stay on the right side of it. The other UPs I have been writing as if Uttar Pradesh were Lucknow plus Purvanchal plus Kashi, which is how it looks from my family’s charpai. It is not how it looks from Meerut, or Jhansi, or Sonbhadra. The state is at least five countries stitched together, and a person from the east can travel for a day inside it and arrive somewhere where he is, in every sense but the passport, a foreigner. Cane country Western UP, the upper Doab between the Ganga and the Yamuna and the districts north of Delhi, is the state’s richest farmland and, not coincidentally, its most self-confident. It is canal country: the British dug the Ganges Canal in the 1850s, and the Green Revolution of the 1960s arrived here early, with tube wells, fertiliser and high-yielding wheat. Its crop is sugarcane, and UP grows more of it than any other state; the cane goes to hundreds of mills whose late payments, the notorious cane arrears, have decided more elections in the west than any temple. Its dominant community of cultivators are the Jats, farmers of the western plains who have never considered themselves anyone’s subjects, and whose leader Charan Singh built the first non-Congress government in the state in 1967 and briefly became prime minister in 1979. The west has its own tradition of protest, and it is louder than the east’s. In October 1988 Mahendra Singh Tikait of the Bharatiya Kisan Union brought hundreds of thousands of farmers from western UP to camp for a week on the lawns of the Boat Club in the heart of Delhi, with their tractors, bullock carts and hookahs, until the government negotiated. In November 2020, when the central government passed three laws to open up agricultural markets, the farmers of Punjab and Haryana marched on Delhi, and the farmers of western UP camped at the capital’s eastern gate, on the highway at a place that happens, by one of those coincidences UP specialises in, to be called Ghazipur. In January 2021, when the protest seemed about to collapse, Tikait’s son Rakesh Tikait wept on camera at the Ghazipur border, and by the next morning thousands of farmers from the villages of the west had arrived to sit with him. In October 2021, at Lakhimpur Kheri, a vehicle in a convoy linked to a Union minister’s son drove into a group of protesting farmers; eight people died that day, including four farmers and a journalist. In November 2021 the Prime Minister repealed the laws. Farmers from the state that had given him two landslides had helped to make him retreat. The west also holds the state’s workshops: Moradabad’s brass, Aligarh’s locks, Firozabad’s glass bangles, made in furnaces where children worked for generations, Saharanpur’s carved wood, Meerut’s cricket bats and footballs, Agra’s shoes. And it holds the state’s newest face. NOIDA, the New Okhla Industrial Development Authority, was created in April 1976, during the Emergency, as an industrial suburb for Delhi; half a century later Noida and its neighbour Greater Noida hold glass towers, a film city, an airport at Jewar and one of the largest mobile-phone factories in the world. People in the east call Noida “UP” with the same hesitation people in Geneva feel about calling Geneva “Swiss”. North of the cane country is Rohilkhand, once ruled by Afghan Rohillas, with Bareilly and the old Nawabi court of Rampur, whose Raza Library holds one of the finest collections of Indo-Islamic manuscripts in the world. North of that is the Terai, the forest-and-grassland strip along the Nepal border, where the Tharu people live and tigers still walk out of Dudhwa and Pilibhit into sugarcane fields, to the terror of everyone involved. The dry south Bundelkhand is UP’s other extreme. Seven districts in the south of the state, Jhansi, Lalitpur, Jalaun, Hamirpur, Mahoba, Banda and Chitrakoot, sit on a rocky plateau of granite and thin soil that the Ganga’s gifts never reached. It rains little, and unreliably, and the region has had some of the worst droughts in modern Indian history; in the 2000s and 2010s its villages emptied of young men who left for the brick kilns and building sites of Delhi and Punjab, and its farmers killed themselves in numbers that briefly made national news. The government’s great answer is the Ken–Betwa link, the first project in a national scheme to join rivers, which will carry water from the Ken into the Betwa at the cost of flooding part of a tiger reserve in Madhya Pradesh. Its foundation stone was laid in December 2024. Bundelkhand has heard promises before. It was not always the poor relation. The Chandela kings who built Khajuraho ruled from here, and their fort at Kalinjar, near Banda, was one of the strongest in India. Its great folk epic, the Alha Khand, tells of two warrior brothers, Alha and Udal of Mahoba, who fought for the Chandela king against Prithviraj Chauhan in the twelfth century; it is still sung during the monsoon, at length, by singers who can go on for nights, and villagers say that when it is sung well, the listeners’ blood rises and fights break out. Chitrakoot, on the Mandakini, is where Ram, Sita and Lakshman are believed to have spent much of their exile. Jhansi had its Rani. And the ravines of the Chambal and the Betwa gave UP its dacoits, bandits who were half criminal and half folk hero, from Man Singh to Phoolan Devi to Dadua, killed by the state’s Special Task Force in 2007. And there is the far south-east, which almost nobody mentions. Sonbhadra, on the borders of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand, has coal, cement and giant power stations that light the north, and Adivasi communities, Gonds and others, who have lived on the land for longer than anyone has been keeping records and have rarely been asked about any of it. In July 2019, in the village of Ubbha, ten Gond villagers were shot dead in a dispute over land that their families had farmed for generations. It is also UP. It is simply not the UP anyone puts on a postcard. When I say I am from UP, I mean a very particular part of it. I have learned to say so. The state is too big for anyone to speak for all of it, and the people who try usually turn out to be speaking for their own district. Warp and weft If you want to understand Uttar Pradesh through a single object, you could do worse than a piece of cloth. The state’s history is woven into it, quite literally: the Mughal court’s taste, the Nawabs’ extravagance, the weaver-saints, the colonial collapse of a great industry, Gandhi’s spinning wheel, the mills of Kanpur and their death, the women embroidering in back rooms for a pittance. Kabir was a weaver, and when he wanted to describe the human body and the soul that wears it, he reached for the thing he knew best: झीनी झीनी बीनी चदरिया ॥ … दास कबीर जतन करि ओढ़ी, ज्यों की त्यों धर दीनी चदरिया ॥ jhīnī jhīnī bīnī chadariyā … dās kabīr jatan kari oṛhī, jyoṃ kī tyoṃ dhar dīnī chadariyā Finely, finely woven is this sheet … Kabir wore it with care, and gave it back just as it was. Chikankari Lucknow’s is white. Chikankari is embroidery in white cotton thread on fine white cloth, originally muslin, now also cotton, voile, georgette and anything else that will sell. The city’s favourite story is that it came from Persia with Nur Jahan, Jahangir’s queen; the story is unprovable and probably romantic, but the craft certainly flourished under Mughal and then Nawabi patronage, and by the nineteenth century Lucknow was its capital. It is made in stages, by different hands. A block-printer stamps the design onto the cloth in a fugitive blue dye that will wash out. The embroiderers, almost all of them women, work it with a vocabulary of stitches, traditionally counted at around thirty-two, whose names are a small poem in themselves: tepchi, a long running stitch; bakhia, the shadow-work stitch worked on the back of the fabric so that the thread glows through from behind; phanda and murri, tiny knots like grains of rice; and jaali, in which the threads of the cloth are teased apart, without ever being cut, to open a lace-like net inside the fabric itself. Then the washermen of the Gomti wash out the blue, and the piece is finished. A fine chikan kurta can take weeks. Lucknow chikankari received a Geographical Indication in 2008. Plate 5 Thirty-two stitches, weeks of work, and a wage that would embarrass the boutique. It is also, like so much of what Lucknow is proud of, built on women’s poverty. The embroiderers, mostly Muslim women working at home in the old city and the villages around it, are paid by the piece through chains of middlemen, and the money that reaches them is a sliver of what the kurta sells for in a Delhi boutique. Since the 1980s organisations like SEWA Lucknow have tried to organise them and cut out some of the middle; it is slow work. At weddings I wear a sherwani rather than chikan, but anyone who wears a chikan kurta, in Lucknow or in a Delhi boutique, is wearing somebody’s eyesight. Banarasi Varanasi’s is gold. The Banarasi sari is woven on handlooms in silk, with zari, thread wrapped in gold or silver, brocaded into it in patterns of creepers, flowers and paisleys; the heaviest, the kinkhwab, literally “little dream”, were so dense with metal that they were worn only by royalty. The weavers of the city’s Madanpura and Lohta neighbourhoods are mostly Muslim, from the Ansari community, and the saris they weave are, for a large part of Hindu north India, the thing a bride must wear. There is no better single emblem of the Ganga-Jamuni idea than a Hindu bride in Banarasi silk: she is wearing, on the most sacred day of her life, the work of Muslim hands. Banaras brocades and saris received a Geographical Indication in 2009. And the industry is in trouble. Powerlooms in Surat and elsewhere, and cheap imported silk and synthetic copies, have undercut the handloom for decades; in the 2000s there were reports of weaving families in the city facing hunger and of weavers taking their own lives. The government’s schemes come and go. The looms get quieter. The eastern looms, the carpets and the gold Further east are the looms I grew up around. Mau and Mubarakpur, in Azamgarh, weave saris in silk and cotton that are sold across north India, often under the more famous Banarasi name. Tanda, in Ambedkar Nagar, weaves the cheap, cheerful cotton that becomes towels and gamchhas, the checked cotton cloth every man in the east wears on his shoulder or around his head. Between Varanasi and Prayagraj, in Bhadohi and Mirzapur, is India’s carpet belt, where hand-knotted rugs are made for export to Europe and America; Bhadohi’s carpets received their own Geographical Indication in 2010. In the 1980s and 1990s the belt became internationally notorious for child labour, and campaigns and labelling schemes followed; the problem shrank, though not everyone believes it vanished. In Lucknow and Bareilly, zardozi, heavy embroidery in gold and silver wire, decorates bridal wear and the robes of anyone who wants to look like a Nawab. Farrukhabad and Pilkhuwa print cotton by hand with carved wooden blocks. UP has a textile for every occasion from birth to death, and the shroud is made here too. What the Company did to the looms For most of recorded history, India was the world’s greatest producer of cotton cloth, and the Ganga plain was one of its heartlands. The collapse of that industry in the nineteenth century, when machine-made cloth from Lancashire flooded Indian markets under a tariff regime designed in London, is one of the central events of colonial economic history. Historians still argue about its exact scale and timing; nobody argues that it did not happen. Millions of weavers and spinners, many of them in the towns of the plain, lost their livelihoods and were pushed back onto the land, which is one of the reasons the villages of eastern UP were so crowded, and so ready to send their sons to the Company’s army or its ships. That is the context of Gandhi’s spinning wheel. Khadi, homespun and handwoven, was not only a moral statement about simplicity. It was an economic argument about who should profit from Indian cotton, aimed directly at the mills of Lancashire and at the memory of the looms they had silenced. When Gandhi toured UP for khadi in 1929, he was speaking to districts that still remembered what they had lost. Kanpur, the Manchester that closed And then UP built its own Manchester. Kanpur, the Cawnpore of the British, was a cantonment town on the Ganga that after 1857 became an industrial city. The Elgin Mills opened in 1864, the Muir Mills in 1874, the Cawnpore Woollen Mills, whose Lal Imli blankets warmed half of north India, in 1876. The army’s need for boots, saddles and harness made the city India’s leather capital, and tanneries spread along the river at Jajmau. By the early twentieth century Kanpur was one of the largest industrial cities in India, called, inevitably, the Manchester of the East, with Indian industrial houses like the JKs alongside the British firms, and a militant labour movement to match; its mill workers’ strikes were some of the fiercest in the country. From the 1970s it came apart. The old mills, starved of investment, became “sick”, were nationalised to save jobs, lost money for decades and closed, one after another, through the 1990s and 2000s; Lal Imli, the most famous name of all, stopped producing and became a symbol of the city’s decline. Tens of thousands of mill workers lost their jobs. The tanneries stayed, and so did their effluent, of which more later. Kanpur remains a large and busy city, with IIT Kanpur, defence factories and a thriving small-business economy, but it never became the industrial capital it once promised to be, and a generation of its young men followed the old eastern road: out. Kabir’s sheet is still being woven in UP, by Ansaris in Banaras, by women in Lucknow’s back rooms, by children, sometimes, in Bhadohi, by mill workers who no longer have a mill. Whether it will be given back just as it was is, I suppose, the question for all of them. One language, two scripts, a dozen tongues I grew up speaking at least three languages without being told that any of them was a language. At home in Lucknow and at school we spoke what everyone called Hindi, which was full of Urdu words nobody noticed were Urdu, and in which people said hum for I and tehzeeb for manners. With my grandparents, and in the village, we spoke Bhojpuri, which people in Lucknow called a dialect, with the particular smile that people reserve for a relative who has done well abroad but still eats with his hands. And in the classroom, and later in every office I have ever worked in, there was English, the language of forms, exams and getting out. I have come to think of them as three selves. The Bhojpuri self is funnier and ruder than the others. The Hindustani self is the one that writes poetry, badly. The English self is the one writing this. That tangle is not an accident of my family. It is the linguistic history of Uttar Pradesh in miniature, and it is one of the most consequential stories in modern India. The tongues of the plain The Ganga plain has never had one language. It has had a continuum of related speech that changes every few dozen kilometres, and a few of those forms were written down, polished and turned into literatures. In the west, around Mathura and Agra, was Braj Bhasha, the language of Krishna devotion, of the blind poet Surdas, and of Raskhan, a sixteenth-century Pathan Muslim who wrote some of the most tender verses to Krishna in the language and asked, in one of them, to be reborn as anything at all in Braj — a cowherd, a bird, a stone — so long as it was there. In the middle was Awadhi, in which the Sufi poet Malik Muhammad Jayasi of Jais wrote his Padmavat in 1540, a love story that is also a mystical allegory, and in which Tulsidas, a generation later, wrote the Ramcharitmanas. That the two great classics of Awadhi were written by a Muslim mystic and a Hindu devotee, in the same language and within a few decades of each other, is the kind of fact UP ought to put on its number plates. In the east was Bhojpuri; in the south, Bundeli; around Kannauj, Kannauji. And around Delhi and Meerut, in the far west of the state, was a plain, workmanlike speech called Khari Boli, the “standing” or “upright” dialect. Amir Khusrau, the thirteenth-century poet and musician, born at Patiali near Etah, is credited with some of the first verses in this Hindavi. Over the next five centuries, in the camps, bazaars and courts of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, it absorbed an enormous Persian and Arabic vocabulary and became the common tongue of north India: Hindustani. Written in the Persian script, with a Persianised literary register, it became Urdu. Written in Devanagari, with a Sanskritised literary register, it became modern Hindi. At the level of the street and the kitchen and the film song, they remained, and remain, one language. The split How one language became two is a story in which UP played the central part. In 1837 the British replaced Persian as the language of the courts in the North-Western Provinces with Hindustani written in the Persian script, which in practice meant Urdu. For a Hindu clerk or petitioner who had learned Devanagari, that was a barrier, and through the second half of the nineteenth century a movement grew in the province to have Hindi in Devanagari recognised as well. Its leading literary figure was Bharatendu Harishchandra of Varanasi, the father of modern Hindi prose and theatre, who wrote in 1877: निज भाषा उन्नति अहै, सब उन्नति को मूल nij bhāṣā unnati ahai, sab unnati ko mūl The progress of one’s own language is the root of all progress. In 1893 the Nagari Pracharini Sabha was founded in Varanasi to promote the script. In 1900 the Lieutenant-Governor, Antony MacDonnell, allowed petitions and court documents to be written in Devanagari alongside Urdu. The decision seems small. It was not. Many Muslim leaders, including the men who led Aligarh after Sir Syed’s death, saw it as the start of their displacement, and the Hindi–Urdu controversy became one of the tracks along which Hindu and Muslim politics in north India diverged. By the 1940s, in UP, you could often tell someone’s religion from the script they wrote their language in. In 1947 the new republic chose Hindi in Devanagari as its official language, and UP, in 1951, made Hindi its own. Urdu, the language of Lucknow’s poets and of a large part of its Muslims, had to wait until 1989 to be declared the state’s second official language, and it has been shrinking in UP’s schools ever since. Premchand, the greatest writer UP has produced, lived through the split and refused to take sides. He began in Urdu, under the pen name Nawab Rai; his first collection of stories was confiscated and burned by the British soon after it appeared, as seditious; he then switched to Hindi, and wrote in both, sometimes the same story twice, for the rest of his life. Godaan, his last complete novel, about a poor peasant’s lifelong wish to own a cow, is the closest thing the Hindi language has to a national epic of the village. I read it at school in Hindi. I discovered only much later that half the words in it I had assumed were Hindi were Urdu, and that Premchand would have found the question of which was which uninteresting. The heartland Independence gave UP a new linguistic role, and a new resentment to go with it. The “Hindi heartland”, which in practice means UP and its neighbours, became the base from which Hindi was pushed as a national language, and the south, Tamil Nadu above all, fought back so fiercely in the 1960s that the plan to make Hindi the sole official language was abandoned. Some of the condescension UP still meets in the rest of India has its roots here: the sense that the heartland tried to make everyone else speak its language, and that it speaks that language, when it comes to live in Chennai or Bengaluru, rather loudly. Meanwhile the heartland’s own languages were being flattened by standard Hindi exactly as it hoped to flatten others. Bhojpuri, spoken by tens of millions in India and across the girmitiya diaspora, is still not among the twenty-two languages recognised in the Constitution, despite decades of demands. Its public face is now mostly a cinema and music industry of cheerful, often crude songs that the middle classes in Lucknow profess to despise and play at every wedding. Awadhi and Braj survive in villages, in the Manas recitations, in the songs women sing at weddings and childbirths. The grandchildren of the people I grew up with will probably speak none of them. I notice that I mind this more than I expected to. The calendar and the stage UP keeps two calendars. One is the government’s, with its Republic Day and its financial year. The other is older and much busier, a year so crowded with festivals, fairs, fasts, processions and recitations that the government’s calendar mostly exists to be interrupted by it. Chhath For people from the east, one festival stands above the rest, and it is not Diwali. Chhath falls six days after Diwali, in the month of Kartik, and it is the festival of the Bhojpuri world: eastern UP, Bihar, the Nepal Terai, and now every city where Purvanchalis have gone to work. It is devoted to Surya, the sun, and to Chhathi Maiya, a mother goddess who protects children. It lasts four days. On the first, the women who will keep the vow, the vratins, bathe and eat a single pure meal. On the second evening they eat a sweet rice pudding, kheer, and a flatbread, and then begin a fast of some thirty-six hours, without food and without water. On the third evening, the whole family goes to the river, or a pond, or a tank dug for the purpose, and the women wade in up to their waists, holding flat winnowing baskets heaped with fruit, sugarcane, coconuts and thekua, hard sweet biscuits of wheat and jaggery, and offer them to the setting sun. They come back before dawn the next morning, stand in the cold water again in the dark, and wait for the sun to rise.
