Plate 6 Chhath, the evening offering: thanks to the setting sun, and the trust that it will come back in the morning. There are things about Chhath that make it unlike almost any other Hindu festival. It honours the setting sun before the rising one, which is to say it gives thanks for the end of the day as well as the beginning. It needs no priest; the women conduct it themselves. It is kept across castes, and its offerings are the humblest things a village produces: a bamboo basket, a sugarcane stalk, a radish, a lamp. Its songs, sung by the women on the way to the river, are among the most beautiful in the Bhojpuri language, and for a generation the voice of Chhath across the whole region was the Bihari folk singer Sharda Sinha, who died in November 2024, as it happens during Chhath itself. Of all the rituals of my childhood, Chhath is the one I think of when I think of the women of my family: standing in the river, in the dark, fasting, silent, holding up a basket of fruit to a sun that has not yet come up, trusting completely that it will. If Kashi taught me that you argue with God out loud, Chhath taught me that you can also just wait for him in the water. Chhath has followed the migrants. It is now celebrated on the Yamuna in Delhi, on the beaches of Mumbai and in the harbour of Port Louis, and politicians in Delhi and Mumbai, who would once have ignored it, now build ghats and declare holidays for it, because the Purvanchali vote has noticed who pays attention. The rest of the year The rest of the calendar is too full to list, so here are the ones that stayed with me. Makar Sankranti, in January, is called simply Khichdi in the east, after the dish of rice and lentils that is cooked and given away; at the Gorakhnath temple in Gorakhpur, a fair grows up around the offering of khichdi to the saint. Holi in Braj lasts for weeks, from the Lathmar Holi of Barsana to the temples of Vrindavan drowned in coloured powder; in Varanasi, on the day before, some people play Holi at Manikarnika with the ash of the funeral pyres, which is the most Banarasi thing I can imagine. The monsoon brings kajri, songs of longing sung by women, above all in Mirzapur and Banaras, and swings hung from the branches of trees. In Kartik, fifteen days after Diwali, comes Dev Deepawali, when Varanasi lights a million lamps along every ghat for the gods who are said to come down to bathe; on the same full moon, Ballia holds the Dadri fair, one of the largest cattle fairs in India. Meerut has the Nauchandi fair, held for centuries near both a temple and a dargah. Lucknow has Muharram, Bada Mangal and Eid. Prayagraj has the Magh Mela every year and the Kumbh every twelve, which UNESCO inscribed in 2017 on its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity. The greatest spectacle, for my money, is across the river from Varanasi at Ramnagar, where the Maharaja of Banaras has sponsored a Ramlila every autumn for some two centuries. It is not performed on a stage. It is performed across the whole town, over a month, with different neighbourhoods standing in for Ayodhya, the forest and Lanka, and an audience of thousands who walk from one scene to the next, many of them sadhus reciting the Ramcharitmanas from memory as the boy-actors speak. The Maharaja watches from the back of an elephant. In 2008 the Ramlila tradition of north India was inscribed on UNESCO’s list of intangible heritage. Ramnagar is its purest surviving form, and its most eccentric. The village stage The courts gave UP kathak and thumri. The villages gave it something louder. Nautanki is UP’s folk musical theatre: melodrama sung in verse, to the beat of the nagada, a huge kettle drum, in open-air performances that go on until dawn. Its two great schools grew up in Hathras and Kanpur, and its stories range from the romances of the Persian tales to the martyrdom of Bhagat Singh. For a long time its women’s roles were played by men. Then came Gulab Bai of Kanpur, who in the 1930s became one of the first women to perform on the nautanki stage, ran her own company, and was awarded the Padma Shri in 1990. Nautanki has been dying for fifty years, killed first by cinema and then by television, and the word itself has come to mean, in everyday Hindi, a melodramatic fuss. But its rhythms are everywhere in Hindi film, which borrowed its heroes, its villains and its sense that a story is not finished until everyone has cried. The east has its own forms. Birha is a folk song tradition of the Ahirs, the cattle-herding Yadav community of eastern UP, sung in competition, with singers improvising verses on everything from the Ramayana to the latest scandal; one of its great modern exponents, Hiralal Yadav of Varanasi, received the Padma Shri in 2019. Chaiti is the song of spring, sohar the song of childbirth, and the women’s wedding songs, the gaari, are affectionate and extravagantly obscene insults aimed at the groom’s family, the one occasion when the bride’s side is allowed to say what it really thinks. Across the border in Bihar, Bhikhari Thakur, a barber by caste, created in the early twentieth century the bidesiya theatre, plays about the men who go away to Calcutta and the women they leave, and the troupes of launda naach, in which men dance women’s roles, carried his plays across the Bhojpuri world. In Bundelkhand, as I have said, they sing the Alha in the rains. And everywhere there is the mushaira and the kavi sammelan, the poetry gathering, Urdu and Hindi, which in UP can still fill a field with thousands of people until three in the morning, applauding a well-turned couplet the way other countries applaud a goal. There are few places left on earth where poets are rock stars. UP is one of them. The table Every Indian abroad eventually becomes a bore about food, and I held out longer than most. Geneva broke me. There are things you can find here, and things you cannot, and the things you cannot are the ones that come back at three in the morning. Lucknow’s slow kitchen The food of Lucknow is the food of the Nawabs, which is to say it is patient. Its great technique is dum, cooking in a pot sealed with dough over a low fire, so that meat and rice and spices steam slowly in their own juices. Its great ambition is softness. The galouti kebab, minced meat so fine it barely holds together, flavoured with dozens of spices, is supposedly the invention of a court cook for a Nawab who had lost his teeth; the family shop in the old city’s Chowk that made it famous, Tunday Kababi, was founded in 1905 by a one-armed cook, tunda meaning one-armed, and has fed Lucknow ever since. The kakori kebab is named after the same small town just outside the city where the revolutionaries robbed the train in 1925, which gives Lucknow the unusual distinction of having named both a kebab and a conspiracy after one village. Then there is the Awadhi biryani, lighter and more fragrant than its Hyderabadi cousin, the nihari eaten with kulcha on winter mornings, the saffron-sweet sheermal bread I have never found in Switzerland, the layered warqi paratha, the kormas. And in winter, only in winter and only early in the morning, makhan malai: milk whipped and left out overnight under the dew until it becomes a foam so light that it disappears the moment it touches the tongue, flavoured with saffron and cardamom and eaten from a leaf. It is sold from carts in the old city before the sun gets high enough to melt it. There is no better description of Lucknow’s nazakat than a food that cannot survive being looked at for too long. Varanasi makes the same thing and calls it malaiyo; the two cities have argued for two centuries about who invented it. Banaras for breakfast Varanasi eats standing up. Breakfast is kachori, fried bread stuffed with lentils, with a sharp potato curry, and a hot jalebi to follow; the evening is tamatar chaat, a spicy, sour tomato mash served in a clay cup. The lassi comes in kulhars, unglazed clay cups you smash afterwards, thick enough to stand a spoon in. The langda mango, which Banarasis consider the only mango, and the Banarasi paan, betel leaf folded around lime, catechu, areca nut and whatever else the paanwala feels you deserve, both received Geographical Indications in 2023, which Banarasis regarded as long overdue. At Holi and Shivratri there is thandai, milk with nuts and spices, and some of it has bhang in it. Shiva is said to approve. Visitors should be cautious. The food of the east And then there is the food of the east, which is the food of poor people made with great intelligence, and which I love more than all the kebabs of Lucknow put together. Its crown is litti chokha: balls of wheat dough stuffed with sattu, roasted gram flour mixed with garlic, ginger, green chilli, mustard oil and pickle masala, baked in the embers of a cow-dung fire until the crust cracks, broken open, soaked in ghee, and eaten with chokha, a mash of fire-roasted aubergine, potato and tomato with raw onion and mustard oil. It is the food of a field worker’s lunch, of a wedding, of a winter night round a fire, and there is nothing in Europe that tastes remotely like it. Sattu itself, stirred into cold water with salt, lemon and roasted cumin, is the summer drink of the east, what a labourer drinks at noon to survive the heat, and what I was given as a child when the loo, the hot wind, came off the plain in May. There is dal-bhaat-chokha, the everyday meal of lentils, rice and mash; dal ki dulhin, dumplings of dough simmered in lentils, whose name means “the bride of the dal”; rasiyaw, rice cooked in jaggery for festivals; thekua for Chhath; roasted gram and puffed rice with jaggery for the journey. And the rest of the state Agra has petha, translucent candied ash gourd, sold by the kilo to tourists who come for the Taj and leave with sugar. Mathura has peda, milk sweets offered to Krishna. Meerut has gajak and rewri, sesame and jaggery brittles for the winter. Malihabad, outside Lucknow, has the dasheri mango, whose orchards Josh Malihabadi grew up among. Allahabad has its guavas, with pink flesh in the good years. Rampur has a court cuisine of its own. Kannauj, which does not make food, makes attar, perfume distilled in copper stills the way it was made in the Mughal age, including mitti attar, which smells exactly like the first rain on dry earth. Food in UP is never only food, of course. It is caste: who may enter the kitchen, who may touch the water pot, who eats with whom, and in the villages of my childhood those rules were still enforced, even if in Lucknow they had softened into habits. It is religion: the meat of one community is the taboo of another, and in recent years what was once a matter of private diet has become a matter for the police. And it is migration: the litti stalls of Delhi, Mumbai and Dubai are run by men from Ballia and Buxar, and Purvanchal travels in their tiffin boxes. I have never yet found a decent litti outside the Bhojpuri world. Some things, it seems, refuse to emigrate. The roll call Every state in India has a list of the famous people it has produced, and every state recites it at the slightest provocation. UP’s is unusual not because it is long, though it is, but because of how many of the names on it belong to the whole country, and how few Indians realise that they came from the same state that they are busy being rude about. The poets Mirza Ghalib, the greatest poet in the Urdu language, was born in Agra in 1797; Delhi claims him because he lived and died there, and Agra has never quite forgiven it. Agra also produced Nazir Akbarabadi, a poet the literary establishment of his day thought vulgar because he wrote about ordinary things — Holi, Diwali, kites, bears, the poverty of old age, the price of flour — and who is now read as the first poet of the Indian street. Akbar Allahabadi wrote satirical verse about the Anglicised gentlemen of his own class that is still funny a century later. Firaq Gorakhpuri, born Raghupati Sahay in Gorakhpur, taught English literature at Allahabad, wrote Urdu ghazals of great tenderness and won the Jnanpith, India’s highest literary prize, in 1969. Josh Malihabadi, from the mango town of Malihabad outside Lucknow, was called the poet of the revolution, emigrated to Pakistan in 1958 and regretted it. Majaz, Kaifi Azmi, Shahryar, and in our own time Munawwar Rana, whose poems about his mother were recited at every mushaira in the state until his death in 2024. In Hindi, the list is even longer and I will stop sooner. Jaishankar Prasad of Varanasi, whose Kamayani is the great philosophical epic of modern Hindi. Suryakant Tripathi ‘Nirala’ and Sumitranandan Pant, who, with Prasad and Mahadevi Verma, made the romantic Chhayavad movement, much of it in and around Allahabad. Maithili Sharan Gupt of Jhansi district, the national poet of the freedom movement. Harivansh Rai Bachchan, who taught English at Allahabad, wrote a doctorate on Yeats at Cambridge and a long poem, Madhushala, about a tavern that is not really a tavern, and whose son is the most famous Indian alive; I share a first name with that son, as do a statistically improbable number of UP boys of my generation, and I have been making the same apology for it since school. Kedarnath Singh, born in a village in Ballia, who won the Jnanpith in 2013. Dushyant Kumar of Bijnor, whose ghazals in Hindi became the anthem of every protest against the Emergency. The storytellers Premchand of Lamhi, just outside Varanasi, is the father of the modern Hindi and Urdu short story and I have said enough about him. Srilal Shukla’s Raag Darbari, about a village college, a cooperative society and a local strongman, remains the funniest and bleakest account of power in rural UP. Kashinath Singh’s Kashi ka Assi is Varanasi in all its abusive, argumentative glory. Qurratulain Hyder, born in Aligarh, wrote in Aag ka Darya, the River of Fire, a novel that runs from the age of the Buddha to Partition and is sometimes called the greatest novel in Urdu. Intizar Husain of Bulandshahr, Rahi Masoom Raza of Gangauli, Rahul Sankrityayan of Azamgarh, who walked to Tibet and brought back manuscripts, Hazari Prasad Dwivedi of Ballia. Most of them wrote, one way or another, about the same thing: the village, the city, the caste, the mosque and the temple, and what happens to people who try to leave. The musicians and the screen I have mentioned Bismillah Khan, Ravi Shankar, Girija Devi and Birju Maharaj. Add the composer Naushad of Lucknow, who scored Mughal-e-Azam and Baiju Bawra and made Hindustani classical music the grammar of Hindi film song; the ghazal singer Talat Mahmood of Lucknow; and Begum Akhtar of Faizabad, to whom I will return. UP gave Hindi cinema Amitabh Bachchan, born in Allahabad in 1942, Naseeruddin Shah of Barabanki, the director Muzaffar Ali, whose Umrao Jaan of 1981 is still the most beautiful film ever made about Lucknow, and the writer Javed Akhtar, who grew up in Lucknow and Aligarh. It also gave Bollywood its favourite setting: the eastern UP small town of guns, weddings, local elections and unexpected philosophy, which the Mumbai film industry has spent twenty years mining for everything from Omkara to a web series called, with admirable frankness, Mirzapur. The scientists This is the list people are most surprised by. The Sushruta Samhita, one of the foundational texts of Indian surgery, with its famous description of rebuilding a nose from a flap of cheek skin, is traditionally said to have been composed by a physician teaching in Kashi. Harish-Chandra, born in Kanpur in 1923 and educated at Allahabad, went on to the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton and became one of the most important mathematicians of the twentieth century, the architect of the theory of representations of Lie groups. Meghnad Saha, whose ionisation equation let astronomers read the temperatures of stars from their spectra, spent fifteen years as a professor at Allahabad and founded the National Academy of Sciences there in 1930. Birbal Sahni founded one of the world’s first institutes of palaeobotany in Lucknow in 1946. Jayant Narlikar, the cosmologist who with Fred Hoyle proposed a rival to the Big Bang, grew up on the campus of the Banaras Hindu University, where his father taught mathematics. IIT Kanpur, founded in 1959, trained a large part of the generation that built India’s software industry and Silicon Valley’s too. The list is interesting less for its length than for its geography: Allahabad, Kanpur, Varanasi, Lucknow, the old university towns of the plain, most of which have since declined. UP produced a remarkable scientific class in the first half of the twentieth century and then spent the second half watching it leave. Allahabad University, which people used to call the Oxford of the East without irony, is now known mostly for the civil service coaching industry that has grown up around it. That, too, belongs on the roll call. The thinkers Finally, the people whose ideas still run the country, which is to say its politics. Ram Manohar Lohia of Akbarpur, the socialist who argued that caste, not only class, was India’s central inequality, and whose disciples, Mulayam Singh Yadav among them, built a political movement on that argument. Acharya Narendra Dev, the Buddhist scholar-socialist who taught at Lucknow and Varanasi. Deendayal Upadhyaya, born near Mathura, the ideologue of the Jana Sangh whose “integral humanism” is the official philosophy of today’s BJP; he was found dead beside the tracks at Mughalsarai station, near Varanasi, in 1968, and in 2018 the station was renamed after him. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan at Aligarh, the founders of the Darul Uloom at Deoband and of the Nadwatul Ulama in Lucknow, Ahmad Raza Khan of Bareilly: the men who shaped how the Muslims of South Asia think about modernity and faith. The socialists, the Hindu nationalists, the Muslim modernists and the Muslim traditionalists all trace their intellectual genealogy to the same few hundred kilometres of the Ganga plain. When people say that UP decides India’s politics, they usually mean the eighty seats. They should also mean the ideas. The present tense The roll call does not end with the dead, and it would be a very Lucknow mistake to write as if it did. The writer I feel closest to, of all the living ones, is Varun Grover. He was born in Himachal, grew up in Lucknow and studied engineering at IIT-BHU in Varanasi, which is to say he is, like me, an engineer who was formed by exactly the two cities this essay is about, and then did something more interesting with it. He wrote the lyrics of Gangs of Wasseypur and the screenplay of Masaan, won a National Award for the song Moh Moh Ke Dhaage, co-wrote Sacred Games, did stand-up comedy that got him into trouble, and in 2023 made his first film as a director, All India Rank, about a boy in 1990s Lucknow sent away to Kota to be ground into an engineer by the coaching factories. I watched it with the uncomfortable feeling of a man reading his own school report. His short protest poem of 2019, written during the citizenship protests, about refusing to show one’s papers, was chanted in streets across the country within weeks. He writes the way Lucknow speaks when it is being honest: soft, funny, and with a knife somewhere in the second line. The biggest literary prize ever won in Hindi went to a writer from UP. Geetanjali Shree, born in Mainpuri in 1957, won the International Booker Prize in 2022 for Ret Samadhi, translated by Daisy Rockwell as Tomb of Sand, a novel about an eighty-year-old widow who, after her husband’s death, refuses to get out of bed, then gets up and goes to Pakistan. It was the first book translated from any Indian language to win the prize. It is also, among many other things, a book about how UP families argue, which is to say constantly, lovingly and at tremendous length. In Hindi poetry, the kavi sammelan circuit has produced a new generation of stars, of whom Kumar Vishwas of Pilkhuwa, near Hapur, is the most famous, filling stadiums with romantic verse and political sarcasm; the lyricist Manoj Muntashir of Amethi has written some of the biggest Hindi film songs of the last decade. The storyteller Neelesh Misra of Lucknow turned radio narration into an art form and founded a rural newspaper, Gaon Connection. In classical music, the great Rampur-Sahaswan singer Rashid Khan of Badayun died in January 2024 far too young, and the folk singer Malini Awasthi of Kannauj has spent her career carrying kajri, chaiti and sohar from village courtyards to national stages. In cinema, beyond Anurag Kashyap and Vishal Bhardwaj, there are the director Tigmanshu Dhulia of Allahabad, who made Paan Singh Tomar and Haasil, a film about student politics at Allahabad University that people from UP still quote to each other; Anubhav Sinha, whose Mulk and Article 15 took on the state’s communal and caste violence directly; and the actor Nawazuddin Siddiqui, from Budhana in Muzaffarnagar, who went from a farming family in western UP to Cannes, and whom the whole of Hindi cinema had spent years casting as the man in the background. And there is the UP that others have written. Vikram Seth’s A Suitable Boy (1993), one of the longest novels in the English language, is set in the early 1950s in a fictional state called Purva Pradesh, whose capital, Brahmpur, on the Ganga, is an unmistakable blend of Varanasi, Allahabad and Lucknow; its central drama is the zamindari abolition I mentioned, and its hardest chapters are about a Hindu–Muslim riot at a temple beside a mosque. For many readers around the world, that fictional state is the only UP they know. It is, I have to admit, a very good likeness. The state is still producing its roll call, and most of it is not famous yet. It is on YouTube in Bhojpuri, on Instagram in Awadhi, in coaching-centre hostels in Prayagraj and Kota, in the notebooks of girls in Ballia who will write the next Aadha Gaon. If I have left out your favourite, the comments are open, and UP has never needed an invitation to argue. UP on screen If you have never been to Uttar Pradesh, you have almost certainly seen it anyway. Hindi cinema has been living off the state for as long as it has existed, Indian streaming television has made its gangsters and village clerks into national celebrities, and Hollywood, when it wants to show a character finding himself in India, has a way of sending him to the Ganga. The courtesan, the Nawab and the bride For its first decades, Bombay cinema’s UP was Lucknow, and Lucknow was the courtesan’s house and the Nawab’s palace. Mughal-e-Azam (1960), set at Akbar’s court, with Naushad’s music, is the grandest of all Hindi films and the story of a prince who loves a dancer his father will not accept. Chaudhvin Ka Chand (1960) and Mere Mehboob (1963) are Lucknow love stories of veils, poetry and mistaken identities. Pakeezah (1972), made over fourteen years by Kamal Amrohi of Amroha, is the most extravagant tribute ever paid to the courtesan culture of the old city. Then, as the old world became history, came the films that looked back at it: Satyajit Ray’s Shatranj Ke Khiladi (1977), Shyam Benegal’s Junoon (1978), set in the rebellion of 1857 in Shahjahanpur, and Muzaffar Ali’s Umrao Jaan (1981). Muzaffar Ali also made Gaman (1978), about a young man from a village near Lucknow who drives a taxi in Bombay and cannot afford to go home, which is the truest film about the bhaiya I know. The biggest UP story Bollywood ever told, though, is one most people do not know came from UP at all. In 1982 Rajshri Productions made Nadiya Ke Paar, a gentle village romance in Awadhi-inflected Bhojpuri, adapted from a novel called Kohbar Ki Shart by Keshav Prasad Mishra, which is set in villages of Ballia district. In 1994 Rajshri remade it, with Madhuri Dixit, Salman Khan, fourteen songs and a dog called Tuffy, as Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!, and it became one of the most successful Indian films of all time, the first Bollywood film reported to have grossed more than a hundred crore rupees. The film that taught a generation of middle-class Indians how to have a wedding began as a story about Ballia. The novel, I am told, has a devastating ending. The film removed it. The badlands From the 2000s, the Bollywood image of UP changed from the Nawab’s palace to the small town with a gun. Vishal Bhardwaj, who grew up in western UP, set Omkara (2006), his Othello, among the political strongmen of the Meerut region, and it may be the best Shakespeare adaptation in any language this century. Ishqiya (2010) went to Gorakhpur. Bunty Aur Babli (2005) sent two small-town con artists out of Fursatganj and Kanpur. And Dabangg (2010), set in a fictional UP town called Lalganj, gave the country Chulbul Pandey, a corrupt, swaggering, sunglasses-wearing, utterly lovable UP policeman, and made the word I have been using throughout this essay into a box-office brand. It was one of the biggest hits of the decade. The rest of India, it turned out, loved dabangai on screen as much as it disliked it in the carriage. Then Anurag Kashyap, who grew up in eastern UP, made Gangs of Wasseypur (2012), a five-hour, two-part gangster epic about three generations of coal-mafia families. It is set in Dhanbad, in Jharkhand, not UP, but it was shot largely in and around Varanasi, including the old fort at Ramnagar, and its world of feuds, railway scrap contracts, country pistols and folk songs is instantly recognisable to anyone from Ghazipur or Mau. It premiered at Cannes and changed what Indian crime films were allowed to be. After it came Raanjhanaa (2013) and Masaan (2015) in Varanasi, Masaan following the son of a family of Doms who burn the dead at the ghats and winning two prizes at Cannes; Mukkabaaz (2017) in Bareilly, about a boxer and caste; Article 15 (2019), a police thriller shaped by the Badaun case; and Gulabo Sitabo (2020), Amitabh Bachchan as a miserly old landlord in a crumbling Lucknow mansion. Kaleen Bhaiya and Phulera Streaming made UP a national obsession. Mirzapur, which began on Amazon Prime Video in 2018, follows the Tripathis, a family who control the carpet trade of Mirzapur and, behind it, the guns and the politics of the region; its patriarch, Akhandanand Tripathi, universally known as Kaleen Bhaiya, carpet brother, became one of the most quoted characters in Indian television. It is violent, lurid, and, to anyone from the east, uncomfortably accurate in its details, from the way a local don talks to a district magistrate to the way a wedding turns into a shooting. It also, I suspect, shaped how millions of young Indians who have never been to UP imagine it. Rangbaaz (2018) retold the story of Shri Prakash Shukla. Paatal Lok (2020) took its detectives to Chitrakoot. And then, in 2020, came Panchayat, about a young engineering graduate from the city who, failing to get anything better, takes a government job as secretary of the village council in Phulera, a fictional village in Ballia district. It is gentle, funny and quietly devastating about the boredom, the pettiness, the kindness and the stubborn dignity of village life, and it became one of the most loved Indian series ever made. I watched the first season in Geneva in a single night, and when a character complained about the bus from Ballia, I laughed so hard my neighbour knocked on the wall. For once, the east was on screen and nobody was shooting anyone. The world’s Ganga Outside India, UP on screen mostly means two things: the Taj Mahal and the ghats of Varanasi. The Taj is everywhere. In Slumdog Millionaire (2008), which won eight Oscars, the young brothers Jamal and Salim pass themselves off as tour guides at the Taj, inventing its history for gullible foreigners and stealing shoes from the visitors while they are inside; it is the funniest sequence in the film and a fair portrait of the Agra tourist economy. In Mira Nair’s The Namesake (2006), the hero’s parents take him to the Taj, and the visit becomes the moment he begins to understand them. Victoria & Abdul (2017), with Judi Dench, told the real story of Abdul Karim, a young Muslim clerk from Agra who was sent to wait at table at Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee in 1887 and became her munshi, her teacher of Hindustani and her closest confidant, to the fury of the entire British court. Varanasi is where Hollywood sends people to be changed. In The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008), David Fincher’s film about a man who ages backwards, there is a brief montage in which Brad Pitt’s Benjamin, at the height of his youth and his loneliness, wanders through Asia; part of it was filmed in 2007 on the ghats of Varanasi by the director Tarsem Singh, with Pitt among the pilgrims, and the story in the city is that the star happily got a shave from a roadside barber between takes. Pitt later said that he had never seen anything like the place. It is, when you think about it, the perfect city for that film: a story about a man moving against the current of time, filmed in the city whose whole purpose is to release you from it. Long before Hollywood, world cinema had found Varanasi. Satyajit Ray set much of Aparajito (1956), the second film of the Apu trilogy, on its ghats, where the boy Apu’s father dies; it won the Golden Lion at Venice. Deepa Mehta’s Water (2005), about the widows of Varanasi in the 1930s, was supposed to be filmed in the city in 2000 until protesters wrecked the sets and drove the production out; she finished it years later in Sri Lanka, and it was nominated for the Oscar for foreign-language film. Mukti Bhawan, released abroad as Hotel Salvation (2016), is about a father who announces that he is going to Varanasi to die, and a son who has to take him; it is funny, and it is the gentlest film I know about the belief I described earlier. And UP has been at the Oscars in its own right, twice, through two documentaries about women. Period. End of Sentence., about women in a village in Hapur district who start making cheap sanitary pads on a small machine, won the Oscar for best documentary short in 2019. Writing with Fire, about Khabar Lahariya, a newspaper run by Dalit women journalists in Bundelkhand who report on rape, mining mafias and corrupt officials from their mobile phones, was nominated for best documentary feature in 2022. They are, I think, the truest films anyone has made about the state. Nobody in either of them gets shot, and nobody visits the Taj. The sound that travelled One more export, because it changed Western popular culture more than any film. In the 1960s, Ravi Shankar, born in Varanasi in 1920, taught the sitar to George Harrison, and Indian music entered the Beatles and, through them, the counterculture; Shankar played at Monterey and Woodstock and became, for a generation of Westerners, the sound of India. Half a century earlier, in 1915, Rabindranath Tagore’s English versions of Kabir, Songs of Kabir, had introduced the weaver of Varanasi to Western readers, and poets from Ezra Pound’s generation to Robert Bly’s have been translating him since. The weaver who mocked every pundit in Kashi now circulates on Instagram in English, usually misattributed, occasionally correct. He would have found this very funny. Ganga, Jamuna, and the canal at Hashimpura In Lucknow the phrase is Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb: the culture of the two rivers, Hindu and Muslim, meeting at Prayag and flowing on together. Lucknowis use it the way the Swiss use the word “consensus”, as a description of how things are and a warning about how they had better stay. It is a real thing. It is also, like consensus, something that has to be made every day, and in UP it has been unmade, violently, more often than anywhere else in India. UP has more Muslims than any other Indian state: the 2011 census counted about 38 million, a little under a fifth of the population, more than live in most Muslim-majority countries. It has more Hindu holy places of the first rank than any other state: Ayodhya, Mathura, Vrindavan, Kashi, Prayag. It produced both of the great rival schools of Sunni Islam in South Asia, the reformist Darul Uloom at Deoband, founded in 1866, and the devotional Barelvi movement of Ahmad Raza Khan of Bareilly; Lucknow’s Firangi Mahal gave the madrasas of the subcontinent their standard curriculum for two centuries. It has three of Buddhism’s four holiest sites. And it has, running through all of it, a deep layer of shared devotion that belongs to no single religion at all. The shared shrines That layer is easy to find if you look. At Dewa Sharif, near Barabanki, the shrine of the Sufi saint Haji Waris Ali Shah, Hindus and Muslims play Holi together in the courtyard every year, throwing colour at a Muslim tomb. In Lucknow’s Aliganj, the city’s best-loved Hanuman temple was, by the most common account, built in the eighteenth century by a begum of the Nawab’s household after a vow for a son was answered, and some old accounts say its spire once carried the Islamic crescent; Accounts of the Aliganj Hanuman temple differ on which begum built it and on whether its spire carried a crescent. Treat both as the city’s tradition. the festival of Bada Mangal, when the whole city sets up free food stalls on the Tuesdays of the month of Jeth, began there, and Muslims set up stalls too. In Varanasi, the Ramlila effigies are traditionally made by Muslim craftsmen, the saris for Hindu weddings are woven by Muslim families, and the shehnai that played at the temple every dawn for decades was Bismillah Khan’s. At the dargah of Ghazi Miyan in Bahraich, Hindu pilgrims came for centuries. Raskhan wrote for Krishna, Rahim wrote dohe on Ram, Rahi Masoom Raza wrote the words of the Mahabharat, Kabir mocked everyone equally. I grew up inside a version of this without thinking about it. None of it felt like tolerance. Tolerance is what you extend to strangers. This was just the neighbourhood. The breaking points And yet. The same state has one of the longest and bloodiest records of communal violence in India, and a history of honesty requires the list. In 1893, a wave of riots over cow slaughter swept the eastern districts, including Mau, one of the first mass Hindu–Muslim riots of the colonial era; the cow has been a trigger in the east ever since. In March 1931 Kanpur burned for days, and Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi died in it. On the night of 22 December 1949 idols of Ram were placed inside the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya, a sixteenth-century mosque on a site that many Hindus believed was Ram’s birthplace; the district officials declined to remove them, the mosque was locked, and a legal dispute began that would last seventy years and reshape the republic. The riots of independent India followed a grim pattern, often with the state’s own armed police, the Provincial Armed Constabulary, as a participant rather than a referee. In Moradabad in August 1980, police fired into a crowd of Eid worshippers at the Idgah, and the riots that followed killed scores, by some counts hundreds. On 22 May 1987, during riots in Meerut, men of the PAC rounded up Muslim men from the Hashimpura neighbourhood, drove about forty-two of them to the edge of a canal The number killed at Hashimpura is given as forty-two in most accounts. A few men survived by pretending to be dead, and their testimony was central to the conviction thirty-one years later., shot them and threw the bodies into the water. It took thirty-one years for a court, the Delhi High Court in 2018, to convict sixteen former policemen of the killings; by then several of the accused, and many of the families, were dead. The next day, in the village of Maliana nearby, dozens more were killed. Then came the mobilisation to build a Ram temple on the site of the Babri Masjid. In October and November 1990, the police of Mulayam Singh Yadav’s government fired on kar sevaks, Hindu volunteers, trying to reach the mosque, killing at least sixteen by the official count and many more by the movement’s. On 6 December 1992, in front of the police, political leaders and the cameras, a crowd of kar sevaks tore the mosque down with hammers and bare hands in a few hours. The riots that followed across India, in Mumbai above all, killed some two thousand people. In November 2019 the Supreme Court awarded the site to the Hindu side, while describing the placing of the idols in 1949 and the demolition in 1992 as illegal, and ordered land elsewhere for a mosque. On 22 January 2024 the Prime Minister consecrated the new temple. Four and a half months later, in the general election, the voters of the Faizabad constituency, which includes Ayodhya, elected the opposition’s candidate, a Dalit politician from the Samajwadi Party. UP rarely gives anyone the ending they expect. The list does not end there. In September 2013 riots in and around Muzaffarnagar, in western UP, killed more than sixty people and drove tens of thousands of Muslims from villages where their families had lived for generations; many never went back. In September 2015, in Bisara village near Dadri, a mob killed Mohammad Akhlaq over a rumour that his family had beef in their fridge, and the word “lynching” entered India’s political vocabulary. In December 2019, protests against the new citizenship law left some twenty people dead in UP, most of them from police gunfire, according to reporting at the time. In November 2024 in Sambhal, a court-ordered survey of the old Jama Masjid, on a petition claiming it stood on a temple, led to clashes in which at least four men were killed. In Varanasi the Gyanvapi mosque and in Mathura the Shahi Idgah remain in court, each with a petition claiming the land beneath it. The palimpsest on the Allahabad pillar was left alone for two thousand years. The palimpsests in stone and brick are being litigated, surveyed and, sometimes, fought over. It is not only religion. Caste has its own list: the Dalit villagers killed by upper-caste men at Shabbirpur near Saharanpur in 2017, the young Dalit men from western UP who formed the Bhim Army in response and whose leader now sits in Parliament. And it is not only between communities. The Shia–Sunni tensions of Lucknow, the Barelvi–Deobandi quarrels, the upper-caste rivalries that fuel the gangs of the east: UP has always had enough conflict to go round. What the rivers actually do Here is what I have come to think, having read far more about this than I did as a boy eating sevaiyan. Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb is not a myth, and it is not a guarantee. It is a practice, kept alive by people who have a reason to keep it: weavers and traders who need each other’s custom, neighbours who need each other’s help, poets who need each other’s words. It survives where those reasons survive. Riots, in UP as elsewhere, have rarely erupted spontaneously from ancient hatreds; again and again, the commissions of inquiry and the historians have found an organised spark, an election, a procession routed down the wrong lane on purpose, a rumour spread on purpose, and a police force that chose which side to stand on. The rivers meet at Prayag because of geography. The cultures met because people worked at it. When people stop working at it, or are paid to stop, the confluence becomes a border. The rivers meet at Prayag because of geography. The cultures met because people worked at it. Bahubalis: guns, votes and encounters In Ghazipur, when I was growing up, there was one name that people lowered their voices to say, and it belonged to a man who was, for most of that time, in jail. Mukhtar Ansari was born in 1963 in Mohammadabad, the same small town where the eight men of Sherpur were shot in 1942. His family was, by any measure, distinguished. His paternal grandfather, Mukhtar Ahmed Ansari, was a doctor, a president of the Indian National Congress and a founder and chancellor of the Jamia Millia Islamia in Delhi. His maternal grandfather, Brigadier Mohammad Usman, was killed in the first war over Kashmir in 1948 and decorated with the Mahavir Chakra. A former Vice-President of India, Hamid Ansari, is his uncle. The family home in Mohammadabad was known simply as the Phatak, the gate, and the story in the town is that the poor who knocked on it rarely went away empty-handed. Mukhtar played cricket for his college in Ghazipur, went into student politics, and by the 1990s was fighting a gang war across Ghazipur, Mau and Varanasi with a rival, Brijesh Singh, over the railway, coal and government contracts that are the real economy of the east’s crime. He was elected to the state assembly from Mau five times, twice for Mayawati’s BSP, the last three times from inside prison. In November 2005, while he was in jail, Krishnanand Rai, the BJP legislator who had taken the Mohammadabad seat from his brother, was ambushed on a road near the town and killed with six others; the police reportedly counted some sixty bullet holes in Rai’s body. Mukhtar spent the rest of his life in prison. He was convicted in eight cases after 2022, including, in 2023, over the murder of Rai, and died of a cardiac arrest in Banda jail on 28 March 2024, aged sixty. His family said he had been slowly poisoned; the post-mortem said heart attack; a magisterial inquiry was ordered. Thousands followed his body to the family graveyard in Mohammadabad. A few weeks later his brother Afzal was elected to Parliament from Ghazipur. I tell the story not because it is exceptional but because it is not. Almost every district in eastern UP has its version: a family with a proud history, a young man with charisma, a contract worth fighting over, a caste or community rival, a murder, an election won, a prison cell with air coolers, a funeral attended by thousands. The Ansari–Rai feud was, on one level, a Muslim family against a Bhumihar one, and it was very easy for politicians to make it into a religious story. It was, on another level, simply two gangs fighting over money, and the religion was paint. How crime learned to vote The word for such men in UP is bahubali, the strong-armed one, and they were a political invention before they were a criminal one. In the 1970s and 1980s, as the Congress lost its grip on UP, politicians began to rely on local strongmen to deliver votes, sometimes at gunpoint, and the strongmen noticed that they no longer needed the politicians. In 1985 Hari Shankar Tiwari of Gorakhpur, the leader of the Brahmin side of a violent Brahmin–Thakur rivalry that had begun in the Gorakhpur University student union, is said to have become the first man in India to win an election from inside a jail. After that the model spread. In the 1990s a young gangster in Gorakhpur called Shri Prakash Shukla became so dangerous, and was rumoured to have taken a contract on the Chief Minister himself, that the state, under Kalyan Singh’s BJP government, set up a Special Task Force largely to hunt him. Its first chief, Ajay Raj Sharma, handpicked the officers, among them an SSP named Arun Kumar, and on 22 September 1998 they shot Shukla dead in Ghaziabad, the STF’s first famous encounter. In Allahabad Atiq Ahmed won the city West seat five times and, in 2004, the Phulpur Lok Sabha seat that Jawaharlal Nehru once held. In Pratapgarh the Kunda seat has been held since 1993 by a former royal known to everyone as Raja Bhaiya. The political scientist Milan Vaishnav, in a 2017 book called When Crime Pays, argued that Indian voters choose candidates with criminal records not out of ignorance but because, where the state is weak and courts are slow, a man who can get things done by any means is a rational choice; he is also often from their own caste, and will protect them in a world where no one else will. UP is the textbook case. In the assembly elected in 2022, about half the members had declared criminal cases against themselves, according to the Association for Democratic Reforms, and a large share of those were serious. That is not a fringe. That is the chamber. Four chief ministers and their strongmen Every government in Lucknow for thirty years has promised to end gunda raj, and every one has, sooner or later, found a strongman it could live with. The only fair way to judge them is side by side. Mulayam Singh Yadav, Netaji to his party, was chief minister three times: 1989 to 1991, 1993 to 1995 and 2003 to 2007. He built the Samajwadi Party on the backward classes and Muslims who had been at the bottom of the old order, and many of them remember his governments as the first in which the police station did not automatically take the landlord’s side. His opponents remember something else. His last term, above all, became a byword for criminals under political protection. In January 2005 Raju Pal, a newly elected BSP legislator in Allahabad, was shot dead in the street; the man accused of ordering it was Atiq Ahmed, then a Samajwadi MP. Within days of Mulayam’s return to power in 2003, his government moved to drop the anti-terror charges that Mayawati had brought against Raja Bhaiya, until the courts stopped it. By 2007 gunda raj was the main charge against him, and Mayawati had the slogan for it: chadh gundon ki chhati par, mohar lagegi haathi par, climb on the chest of the goons and stamp the elephant. Mayawati won that election outright, and her government of 2007 to 2012 is remembered, even by many who dislike her, as the one that most visibly jailed strongmen, including her own. In 2002, in an earlier term, she had sent Raja Bhaiya to jail under the anti-terror law. In 2007, weeks into her new term, she had Umakant Yadav, a BSP MP from Azamgarh accused of grabbing a farmer’s land, arrested by the Director General of Police, Vikram Singh, at the gate of her own residence. That July the Special Task Force, under a young SSP named Amitabh Yash, killed the Chitrakoot dacoit Dadua, who had ruled the ravines of Bundelkhand for a quarter of a century. When one of her own legislators, Shekhar Tiwari, and his men beat a public works engineer named Manoj Gupta to death in December 2008, the MLA was arrested and is serving a life sentence. And yet the same Mayawati fielded Mukhtar Ansari for Varanasi in the 2009 Lok Sabha election, from jail, and called him a messiah of the poor; he was expelled only in 2010, after mobile phones were found in his cell. Akhilesh Yadav, chief minister from 2012 to 2017, came in promising a cleaner Samajwadi Party. Before the 2012 election he had kept the western UP strongman D. P. Yadav out of it, and in June 2016 he forced the cancellation, three days after it was announced, of the party’s merger with Mukhtar Ansari’s Quami Ekta Dal; the fight with his uncle Shivpal over it helped split the party. His government built some of the most lasting pieces of police infrastructure in the state: the 1090 Women Power Line in 2012, a helpline through which women could report harassment without walking into a police station, and the UP 100 emergency service in 2016, which put police response vehicles on a single number. But his term also contained the Muzaffarnagar riots of 2013; the killing in March 2013 of Zia-ul-Haq, a deputy superintendent of police, in Kunda, after which Raja Bhaiya, by then a minister in Akhilesh’s own cabinet, resigned when he was named in the FIR, a case the Supreme Court sent back to the CBI for further investigation in 2023; and, in June 2016, Jawahar Bagh in Mathura, where an armed sect that had occupied a public park for two years killed the city’s superintendent of police, Mukul Dwivedi, and a station officer, Santosh Yadav, during the eviction, in a clash that left more than twenty dead. In 2017 the BJP campaigned on law and order and won more than three hundred seats. Put the four records side by side and the pattern is less about party than about power. Each government jailed some strongmen and sheltered others; each was harder on the strongmen of its rivals than on its own; and the same few names, Raja Bhaiya, Atiq Ahmed, Mukhtar Ansari, passed through all of them, sometimes in the cabinet, sometimes in a cell. The police officers who did the fighting served every government in turn. Amitabh Yash, who led the Dadua operation under Mayawati, came back to run the Special Task Force under Adityanath. The state’s reply Since 2017 the government of Yogi Adityanath has answered the bahubali with a strongman of its own: the state. The policy has two instruments. The first is the encounter. According to the UP police’s own figures, released at the end of 2025, between March 2017 and December 2025 the police carried out more than 16,000 operations described as encounters, in which nearly eleven thousand accused people were injured, often with bullets to the legs, and 266 were killed, along with eighteen policemen. In 2025 alone, 48 people were killed, the highest in any year of the government. The police say every one was in self-defence. The National Human Rights Commission issued notices to the state as early as 2017, after the Chief Minister was quoted as saying that criminals would be jailed or killed in encounters. The second instrument is the bulldozer. For years, the homes and properties of people accused of crimes, and sometimes of people accused of taking part in protests, were demolished, often within days and usually on the grounds that they had been built illegally. In November 2024 the Supreme Court held that demolishing someone’s home because they are accused of a crime, without due process, is unconstitutional, and laid down procedures to stop it. The officers became public figures in a way UP had not seen before. Prashant Kumar, a 1990-batch IPS officer from Bihar, was made additional director general for law and order in May 2020 and acting Director General of Police from January 2024 to May 2025, promoted over thirteen officers senior to him; press profiles credit him with more than three hundred encounters. Amitabh Yash’s Special Task Force pursued the gangs of the east and killed, among others, Asad Ahmed in 2023. The government makes its case in numbers. It says that heinous crimes, dacoity, robbery, murder, rioting, kidnapping and rape, fell by some 85 per cent between 2016 and 2024, and robberies by more than 80 per cent; that dozens of named mafia leaders and hundreds of their associates were charged under the Gangsters Act; and that property worth more than ₹14,000 crore was seized from them. The National Crime Records Bureau’s figures broadly bear out a fall in several kinds of violent crime, while also showing, in some years, a rise in murders linked to firearms and gang rivalry. The early “anti-Romeo squads” of 2017, sent to patrol parks and colleges against the harassment of women, were welcomed by some and denounced by others as moral policing of couples. The spectacles that defined the policy are well known. In July 2020 Vikas Dubey, a Kanpur gangster whose men had ambushed and killed eight policemen at his village of Bikru, was arrested in Ujjain and killed the next day on the way back to UP when, according to the police, the car carrying him overturned and he tried to escape. In April 2023 Atiq Ahmed’s teenage son Asad was killed in an encounter, and two days later Atiq and his brother, handcuffed and surrounded by police, were shot dead in Prayagraj by three young men posing as journalists, live on television, as Atiq was answering a reporter’s question. Many people in UP, and not only supporters of the government, will tell you that the streets feel safer, that businesses no longer pay protection to the local don, that women can travel after dark in towns where they could not before. Some of that is borne out by the crime figures and some of it is not; much of it is a feeling, and in politics feelings count. Many others will tell you that a state which kills people it has decided are guilty has simply become the biggest bahubali of all, and that the list of the dead is not distributed evenly across castes and religions. I do not think the argument can be settled by the number of bodies on either side of it. A state that answers the gun with the gun has made the gun the argument, and in UP, where the gun has always been the argument, that is not reform. It is continuity in a uniform. A state that answers the gun with the gun has made the gun the argument. The man in the next berth on the night train, the one who knew all the strongmen, is the heart of this. He was not a criminal. He was a schoolteacher, or a clerk, or a contractor, and he knew the strongmen because in the east you had to, the way you had to know which ghat floods first. The bahubali exists because ordinary people need someone to call when the police will not come, the court will take twenty years and the landlord has a gun. Take away the need and the strongman withers. Kill the strongman and leave the need, and another one will be along by the next election. Devi and ghoonghat On the eighth or ninth day of Navratri, in homes all over UP, families invite little girls from the neighbourhood, wash their feet, tie a red thread on their wrists, feed them puri, black chickpeas and halwa, touch their feet and send them home with a coin and a gift. The ritual is called kanya pujan, the worship of the maiden: each girl, for that morning, is the goddess. It is a lovely ritual, and a hard one to watch once you know the numbers. Some of the same households that wash the feet of nine girls on Ashtami have, on the evidence of every census, preferred for generations not to have daughters at all. UP is a state where women are worshipped with extraordinary sincerity and treated, in daily life, with an equally extraordinary lack of it. Both of those are true, and neither cancels the other. The goddesses The state is crowded with them. Ganga herself is Ganga Maiya, Mother Ganga; you do not bathe in her, you are received. On the Vindhya hills above Mirzapur sits Vindhyavasini, one of the most powerful goddess shrines in the north. In Kashi the goddess Annapurna feeds the city and Shiva himself, in one of her best-known images, holds out his bowl to her for alms. Sita is Ayodhya’s daughter-in-law, and in the villages of Awadh the wedding songs still weep for her exile. In Braj it is Radha, not Krishna, whom devotees in Vrindavan greet — Radhe Radhe is the local hello — and at Barsana, her village, the women celebrate Holi by beating the men of the neighbouring village with long bamboo sticks while the men hide behind shields: the Lathmar Holi, the one day of the year when UP officially lets women hit men, and does so with great enthusiasm. The goddess in UP is not a gentle abstraction. Durga kills a buffalo demon; Kali drinks blood. The tradition has always known that the feminine can be ferocious. What it has been less willing to accept is that an actual woman, a daughter-in-law, say, might be. What the history records The history is, as usual, both better and worse than the ritual. The early Buddhist texts remember, at Shravasti, a laywoman called Visakha, a merchant’s daughter-in-law who defied her father-in-law, funded a great monastery and was consulted by the Buddha himself; Buddhism, whatever its own hesitations, created an order of nuns whose poems, the Therigatha, are among the oldest writing by women anywhere. The Mughal court gave Agra Nur Jahan, who issued coins in her own name, ran much of the empire for her husband Jahangir, and built her father’s tomb, the jewel-box of Itmad-ud-Daula, which anticipated the Taj. Awadh had Bahu Begum of Faizabad, the Nawab’s widow, whose private fortune was so large that the East India Company’s Warren Hastings had her household coerced into surrendering much of it; the abuse of the “Begums of Oudh” became one of the charges in his impeachment in London. In 1857 the rebellion in Lucknow was led, in her son’s name, by Begum Hazrat Mahal; Jhansi’s was led by Lakshmibai; and alongside them fought women the textbooks took a century to notice. Jhalkari Bai, a woman of the Kori weaving caste, is said to have disguised herself as the Rani to draw off British troops. Uda Devi, a Pasi woman, climbed a pipal tree at the Sikandar Bagh in Lucknow and is said to have shot dead a number of British soldiers before she was killed; the British officers who found her body recorded their astonishment that the sniper had been a woman. Both are now heroines of Dalit politics, and Mayawati put up their statues. Azizunbai, a courtesan of Kanpur, is remembered as having ridden with the rebels, armed, in men’s clothes. Against that, the patriarchy of the plain was deep and in some places murderous. In 1789 Jonathan Duncan, the Company’s Resident at Benares, reported that among certain Rajput clans in Jaunpur and the surrounding districts it was customary to kill infant daughters at birth, and found villages in which almost no girls survived; the practice persisted long enough that the British passed a Female Infanticide Prevention Act for the region in 1870. Purdah, among the Muslim upper classes and the Hindu ones who imitated them, kept respectable women indoors and silent; the ghoonghat, the veil drawn over a married woman’s face in the presence of her husband’s elders, still marks the village daughter-in-law across the state. Girls were married as children. Widows, above all upper-caste widows, were forbidden to remarry, shaved, dressed in white and, in their thousands, sent to live out their lives on alms in Vrindavan and Kashi. The courtesans whose music Lucknow celebrates were, as I have said, often girls who had been trafficked as children. The women who walked out What makes UP’s twentieth century remarkable is the number of women who walked out of that world and held the door open for others. Rashid Jahan, a doctor from an Aligarh family, co-wrote Angaaray, Embers, in 1932, a collection of Urdu stories so frank about sex, religion and the lives of women that it was banned within months and its authors were threatened; she spent the rest of her short life treating poor women and organising progressive writers. Ismat Chughtai, born in Badayun in 1915, wrote Lihaaf, The Quilt, a story about a neglected begum and her maidservant, and was tried for obscenity in Lahore in 1944; she refused to apologise, won, and went on to write for a further forty years with exactly the same lack of apology. Mahadevi Verma, the great poet of the Chhayavad movement, published in 1942 a book of essays on the condition of Indian women, Shrinkhala ki Kadiyan, The Links of the Chain, that is still one of the sharpest feminist texts in Hindi, and ran a college for women in Allahabad for decades. Subhadra Kumari Chauhan, born in Allahabad, wrote the poem about the Rani of Jhansi that every Hindi-speaking child still learns by heart. Qurratulain Hyder won the Jnanpith in 1989. Akhtaribai Faizabadi, the singer the world knows as Begum Akhtar, grew up in the milieu of the courtesans, gave up singing in public after her marriage because her husband’s class considered it improper, fell seriously ill, and was told by her doctors that she should sing again. She did, and became the queen of the ghazal. In politics the list is even more striking for a state so often dismissed as backward. Sarojini Naidu became India’s first woman governor, of UP, in 1947, and died in office in Lucknow. Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit of Allahabad became the first woman president of the United Nations General Assembly in 1953. In 1963 Sucheta Kriplani became Chief Minister of UP, the first woman to head any Indian state. Indira Gandhi, born in Allahabad, sat for Rae Bareli. And in 1995 Mayawati, the daughter of a clerk from a Dalit family, became the first Dalit woman to lead any Indian state, and went on to do it four times; whatever one thinks of her statues and her governments, a Dalit woman ruling the state of the Nawabs and the Brahmins of Kashi was a revolution the old order had not imagined. Some of the women who broke free did it violently. Phoolan Devi, a Mallah girl from the ravines of Jalaun, married off at eleven, abused, kidnapped by dacoits and, by her account, gang-raped by upper-caste men in the village of Behmai, returned in February 1981 at the head of her own gang; twenty-two Thakur men of the village were lined up and shot. She surrendered in 1983, spent eleven years in jail without trial, was elected to Parliament from Mirzapur in 1996 and was shot dead outside her Delhi home in 2001. She is a heroine to some and a murderer to others, and she is both. In 2006, in Banda in Bundelkhand, a woman named Sampat Pal started the Gulabi Gang, women in pink saris carrying lathis, who confront abusive husbands and corrupt officials in person. The state that gave India its most celebrated sari-clad goddess with a weapon also gave it the first sari-clad women’s militia with bamboo sticks. There is a pattern there. And now The present is mixed, and the numbers need care, because UP is so large that its absolute totals almost always look terrible. In 2023, according to the National Crime Records Bureau, UP registered about 66,000 crimes against women, more than any other state and nearly fifteen per cent of the national total; measured as a rate per head, it ranked thirteenth of twenty-eight states, below several states with far better reputations. Reported crime depends on whether women go to the police and whether the police write it down, so neither the total nor the rate tells the whole story. The cases that defined the decade tell another. In Unnao in 2017, a teenage girl accused a sitting BJP legislator, Kuldeep Singh Sengar, of raping her; her father died in police custody after being beaten, and it took a self-immolation attempt outside the Chief Minister’s house and the Supreme Court’s intervention before Sengar was convicted in 2019. In Hathras in September 2020, a nineteen-year-old Dalit woman was assaulted in a field and died of her injuries two weeks later; the police cremated her body in the middle of the night, without her family’s consent, and in 2023 a court convicted one of the four accused of culpable homicide and acquitted the other three; none was convicted of rape. The demography is improving slowly. The 2011 census counted 912 women for every thousand men in UP, and only 902 girls for every thousand boys under six. In the National Family Health Survey of 2019–21 about one in six women in UP aged twenty to twenty-four had been married before eighteen, still too many, but a fraction of the rate a generation before. Far fewer women than men work for pay, one of the lowest shares in the country, and a woman in a village in the east still often cannot leave the house without a reason and a male relative. And yet something has shifted, and you can see it at the polling booth. In the sixth phase of the 2024 general election, women in UP voted at about 57 per cent against 51 per cent for men. Every party now designs schemes for women voters, from free gas cylinders to cash transfers, because they have noticed who turns up. In 2022 the Congress fought the state election on the slogan ladki hoon, lad sakti hoon, I am a girl, I can fight, and gave forty per cent of its tickets to women; it won two seats. The women voted anyway, mostly for someone else. They are no longer a bloc that follows the men of the household, and every politician in Lucknow knows it. The young women I knew growing up in Lucknow are doctors, engineers, civil servants, entrepreneurs. The Indian cricketer Deepti Sharma grew up in Agra, playing with the boys. In Lucknow and Agra, cafés run by survivors of acid attacks serve coffee to people who would once have looked away. The goddess is still worshipped. The daughter-in-law still draws the ghoonghat in the village. And the daughter is, more and more often, simply leaving: for college, for Delhi, for work, for a life. UP has always been good at worshipping women. It is only now, slowly and against resistance, learning to get out of their way. UP has always been good at worshipping women. It is only now learning to get out of their way. The road to Delhi Every Indian political journalist has written the sentence, and so, it seems, must I: the road to Delhi runs through Lucknow. It is a cliché because it is true. Of the fourteen people who have served as India’s prime minister, not counting caretakers, nine were either born in UP or sat in Parliament for a UP constituency: Jawaharlal Nehru for Phulpur, Lal Bahadur Shastri, born at Mughalsarai, for Allahabad, Indira Gandhi for Rae Bareli, Charan Singh for Baghpat, Rajiv Gandhi for Amethi, V. P. Singh for Fatehpur, Chandra Shekhar for Ballia, Atal Bihari Vajpayee for Lucknow, and Narendra Modi, a Gujarati who chose, in 2014, to stand from Varanasi, precisely because he understood the sentence. No party has ever governed India comfortably without doing well in UP, and every party that has done very well in UP has governed India. Three revolutions The state’s political history since independence is, roughly, three revolutions and their consequences. The first was the Congress’s, and it was a revolution of continuity. For twenty years UP was run by Nehru’s colleagues — Govind Ballabh Pant, Sampurnanand, Chandra Bhanu Gupta, Sucheta Kriplani — on a coalition of upper castes, Dalits and Muslims, held together by the prestige of the freedom movement and the patronage of the state. It began to crack in 1967, when Charan Singh, the voice of the Jat and middle peasant of western UP, walked out and formed the first non-Congress government. It broke in 1975, when on 12 June Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha of the Allahabad High Court, hearing a petition by the socialist Raj Narain, set aside Indira Gandhi’s election from Rae Bareli for electoral malpractice. Thirteen days later she declared the Emergency. In 1977, when elections came, Raj Narain beat her in Rae Bareli. The most consequential judgment and the most consequential defeat in Indian democratic history both came out of UP within two years. The second revolution was of caste, and it had two wings. The first grew from Lohia’s socialism, argued that the backward classes — the Yadavs, Kurmis, Lodhs and dozens of others who worked the land that upper castes owned — should have power in proportion to their numbers, and found its leader in Mulayam Singh Yadav, a wrestler and schoolteacher from Etawah who founded the Samajwadi Party in 1992. It was given national force when V. P. Singh, in 1990, implemented the Mandal Commission’s recommendation of reservations for the Other Backward Classes in central government jobs. The second wing was Dalit. Kanshi Ram, a Punjabi Dalit government chemist, founded the Bahujan Samaj Party in 1984 with the argument that the Dalits and the most marginalised of the backward classes, a clear majority of Indians, had only to organise to rule. In UP they did. In 1993 the two wings joined to defeat the BJP; in 1995, after a notorious incident in which SP workers besieged Mayawati in a Lucknow guest house, they split and remained enemies for a quarter of a century. In 2007 Mayawati won an outright majority on the most unlikely coalition in Indian politics, Dalits and Brahmins together, the top and bottom of the ladder against the middle. Whatever else it achieved, the caste revolution changed who sat in the assembly in Lucknow more thoroughly than anything since independence. It is why my village’s constituency is represented by a Rajbhar and not a Pathan zamindar. The third revolution was Hindu nationalism, and UP was its heartland in every sense. The Ram temple movement, launched in the 1980s, turned Ayodhya into the centre of national politics. The BJP formed its first government in UP under Kalyan Singh in 1991, and was in power when the mosque came down in 1992. For the next twenty years the party struggled in a state divided among castes. Then, in 2014, the BJP and its allies won seventy-three of UP’s eighty Lok Sabha seats, stitching together upper castes with the non-Yadav backward classes and the non-Jatav Dalits whom the SP and BSP had, in their own ways, taken for granted. In 2017 it won the assembly with more than three hundred seats and made Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, the head priest of the Gorakhnath monastery in Gorakhpur, a monk in saffron who now governs more people than all but five of the world’s countries. He won again in 2022, the first chief minister to be re-elected after a full term in more than three decades. The elephant turns And then, in June 2024, UP surprised everybody again. The Samajwadi Party, now led by Mulayam’s son Akhilesh, campaigned on a formula it called PDA, pichhde, Dalit, alpsankhyak, backward classes, Dalits and minorities, and on fears that the constitution and reservations were at risk. It won thirty-seven seats to the BJP’s thirty-three, including, as I mentioned, Faizabad, and those losses in UP were a large part of why the BJP lost its outright majority in Parliament for the first time in a decade. The next assembly election is due early next year. Everyone in Lucknow is already arguing about it, which is to say that everyone in Lucknow is doing what they always do. The point is not who wins. It is that UP has, in eighty years, produced both of the great ideas that now fight for the country’s soul: the idea that India is at heart a Hindu nation, and the idea that India is at heart a society of castes, each of which must be given its share. Both were made on this plain. Both have governed it. Both, in their purest forms, frighten the other half of the state, and the state keeps oscillating between them like a very large and very sensitive instrument. When people outside UP complain that it decides India’s politics, they are right. They should also understand that UP’s politics is India’s argument with itself, turned up to full volume. UP’s politics is India’s argument with itself, turned up to full volume. Ganga Maiya’s burden The river has come up in almost every section of this essay, as a goddess, a highway, a border, a place to die and a place to wait for the sun. It is time to talk about it as what it also is: a river, and a very sick one. The Ganga flows for more than a thousand kilometres through Uttar Pradesh, a longer stretch than in any other state, and on the way it receives the sewage of Kanpur, Prayagraj, Varanasi and hundreds of towns, the effluent of tanneries, sugar mills, distilleries and paper factories, the runoff of fertiliser from the richest farmland in India, and the ashes, and sometimes the unburned remains, of the dead. The Yamuna, which joins it at Prayagraj, arrives already carrying the waste of Delhi and much of Haryana, and at Agra and Mathura it is, for much of the year, less a river than a slow stream of effluent with foam on it. The Supreme Court had to intervene in the 1990s, in a case brought by the lawyer M. C. Mehta, to create a protected zone around the Taj Mahal and close or move polluting industries, because the air was turning the marble yellow. The worst stretch has long been Kanpur, where the tanneries of Jajmau, the heirs of the city’s leather industry, discharged chromium-laden waste into the river for decades, and where campaigners have photographed the water turning colours no river should be. Varanasi, the holiest stretch of all, takes in the drains of a city of more than a million people; the Assi, which gave the city half its name, is now effectively a sewer. The cleanups have been announced with great ceremony. In 1986 Rajiv Gandhi launched the Ganga Action Plan in Varanasi. In 2014 the new government made the river a national mission, Namami Gange, with a budget of thousands of crores, new sewage plants, rebuilt ghats and a minister for the river. Some of it has worked: there are more treatment plants, some drains have been diverted, the ghats are cleaner than I remember them. Much of it has not. Measurements of faecal bacteria downstream of the big cities still often exceed, by a very large margin, the standard considered safe for bathing, and millions bathe anyway, because the river is not only water. The most moving figure in this story, for me, was Veer Bhadra Mishra, the hereditary high priest of Varanasi’s Sankat Mochan temple, who was also a professor of hydraulic engineering at the Banaras Hindu University, and who spent the last decades of his life campaigning, with data, for the river his temple worshipped. He saw no contradiction between measuring the coliform count and bowing to the goddess. Neither do I. You can believe the river is a mother and also insist that nobody pour sewage into their mother. You can believe the river is a mother and also insist that nobody pour sewage into her. Flood, sand and poison In the east, the rivers are not only polluted; they move. The Ganga, the Ghaghra, the Rapti and the Gandak flood almost every monsoon, and in Gorakhpur, Ballia and Ghazipur the floods are not news but a season. The rivers also eat land. In Ballia, whole villages on the banks have been swallowed by erosion over the decades, and their people rebuilt further back, again and again. The new land the rivers deposit, the sandbanks and silt islands called diara, is fertile and unclaimed and fiercely contested, and some of the east’s oldest feuds, and a few of its gangs, began as fights over diara that did not exist the year before. The water under the ground is not safe either. Ballia and the neighbouring districts sit on some of the worst arsenic contamination of groundwater in India, poison leached naturally from the sediments of the plain into the hand-pumps that villages switched to, in the name of safety, from the old open wells. The skin lesions it causes are a familiar sight in parts of the district. The heat is getting worse: in June 2023, during a heatwave, dozens of people died over a few days in and around the district hospital in Ballia, and the state argued for weeks about whether the heat had killed them. And there is the memory nobody in the east likes to talk about. In May 2021, at the height of the second wave of the pandemic, bodies began to wash up on the banks of the Ganga at Buxar in Bihar and at Gahmar and elsewhere in Ghazipur, and shallow graves were found in the sand along the river at Unnao and Prayagraj. Families who could not find wood, or afford it, or reach a crematorium, had given their dead to the river, or to the sand. For people who believe what I described in the section on Kashi, it was not only a public health disaster. It was a spiritual one. The river that was supposed to carry the dead to liberation had been asked to carry more than it could bear. The air, finally. In winter the whole Ganga plain lies under a brown lid of smoke from crop burning, brick kilns, traffic and a hundred million cooking fires, and cities like Ghaziabad, Noida, Kanpur and Lucknow regularly appear on lists of the most polluted places on earth. In Geneva I check the air quality in Lucknow the way other people check the weather at home. It is not a habit I recommend. The Gangetic river dolphin, a blind, ancient creature that finds its way by sound, still survives in parts of UP’s stretch of the river, and in 2009 India made it the national aquatic animal. It is, I think, the right symbol. It cannot see the water it lives in. It has to listen for what is there. So, increasingly, do we. The elephant nobody invites In the mid-1980s the demographer Ashish Bose, looking at the states that were dragging down India’s development figures, coined an acronym from their initials: Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh. BIMARU. It was a pun, bimar meaning sick in Hindi, and like all good puns it stuck far longer than its author intended. Forty years later, people still use it, usually without knowing where it came from and always knowing what it means. The numbers behind it have not gone away. In 2024–25 UP’s income per person was about ₹1.09 lakh, roughly half the national average, the second lowest of the large states after Bihar. By one estimate, the state’s output per head is comparable to Nepal’s. And yet UP has the third-largest economy of any Indian state, because there are so many people in it; it grows about a fifth of India’s food grains and is the country’s largest producer of sugarcane and milk. The state is rich in total and poor per person, which is what you get when you divide a large cake among a very large family. Bhaiya The poverty has a human shape, and the rest of India sees it every day. For two centuries the east of UP has sent its young men away to work: to the jute mills of Calcutta, the docks of Bombay, the plantations of Mauritius, the building sites of Delhi and, now, the gig economy of every city in India. The census of 2011 found UP to be the largest source of people living in another state. In Mumbai and Delhi, the word for such a migrant is bhaiya, brother, which on the face of it is affectionate and in practice is often not. In 2008, supporters of Raj Thackeray’s party in Maharashtra beat up north Indian taxi drivers and candidates arriving for railway exams, on the grounds that they were taking Marathi jobs. In March 2020, when the country locked down with four hours’ notice, millions of those migrant workers, suddenly jobless and homeless, began walking home along the highways, many of them to UP and Bihar, and some of them died on the way. The images of that spring are, I think, the truest portrait India has of what the phrase “UP-Bihar” means to the rest of the country: people it depends on and does not see until they leave. The condescension is real: the joke about paan -stained walls, the assumption that anyone from UP is either a politician’s nephew or a gangster’s. It is also, I should admit, reproduced inside the state with great efficiency. Lucknow looks down on Purvanchal, Purvanchal looks down on Bihar, the city looks down on the village, the upper caste on everyone. Nobody in UP has ever needed outsiders to teach them how to feel superior. What is changing The state is changing faster than its reputation, though not as fast as its governments claim. The NITI Aayog’s multidimensional poverty index, which counts deprivations in health, education and living standards rather than income, found that the share of UP’s population in poverty fell from about 38 per cent in 2015–16 to about 23 per cent in 2019–21, one of the largest falls in the country. Expressways now cross the state; one of them, the Purvanchal Expressway, opened in 2021, runs from Lucknow to Ghazipur, and turns the journey of my childhood, the long night train full of opinions, into a five-hour drive. Noida, on Delhi’s edge, has become one of the largest mobile-phone manufacturing hubs on earth. Ayodhya and Varanasi are building for tens of millions of pilgrims; the Kumbh at Prayagraj in early 2025, which the state claimed drew more than six hundred million visits, was one of the largest gatherings in human history, and a stampede on its busiest night killed at least thirty people, a reminder that scale in UP is always both an achievement and a danger. Other things are changing more slowly. In August 2017, dozens of children died over a few days at the government medical college in Gorakhpur, amid a dispute over unpaid bills for the hospital’s oxygen supply; the region had for decades been the epicentre of encephalitis outbreaks that killed thousands of children. The great universities of Allahabad and Lucknow have declined into feeders for the civil service coaching industry, and recruitment exams are regularly cancelled because the papers leak; in 2024, a police constable exam taken by nearly five million candidates had to be scrapped. For many young people in UP, the most realistic route to a good life is still a government job, and the second most realistic is a train ticket.
