why-i-am-twice: Two titles that begin with the same three words. Why I Am a Hindu, by Shashi Tharoor. Why I Am an Atheist, by Bhagat Singh. One is a book of several hundred pages written by a sitting member of parliament with a library at his elbow. The other is a short essay written in a prison cell by a young man who expected to be hanged, and was writing partly to make sure nobody could say afterwards that he had flinched. I did not read them together on purpose. I read one, and then found I could not stop answering it with the other. This essay is where that argument has got to. Plate 1 Two kinds of light, and a man who has read about both. One rule before I start: everything here comes from the two texts and nothing else. It is a harder rule to keep with these two than it sounds. Both men have become symbols, one of a martyr and one of a certain kind of liberal Indian, and a great deal gets said in their names that neither of these texts says. Bhagat Singh’s essay circulates in several versions whose wording differs slightly from one edition to the next; where I quote it, the words may not match your copy exactly, but the arguments will. He wrote it in October 1930, in prison. It was published in The People in September 1931. By then, whether he would pray at the end was no longer a hypothetical question, and the answer was on record. Two defences The first thing worth noticing is that neither text was written in a vacuum. Both are defences. Somebody questioned the author, and the book is the reply. Bhagat Singh tells you exactly who. Some of his friends, he writes, had begun to suggest that his atheism was not a conclusion at all but a symptom: that he had grown vainglorious from the attention of his two trials, the Delhi bomb case and the Lahore conspiracy case, and that a young man who had become famous thought himself too big for God. The essay is his answer to the charge of vanity. It is, in a sense, a document about character before it is a document about theology. Tharoor’s accuser is plural and political. His book is written against two opponents at once. On one side are people who assume that any educated, liberal Indian must have left religion behind, and that a Hinduism worth the name is a bundle of superstitions. On the other side, and much more urgently, are the advocates of Hindutva, who claim to speak for all Hindus and whom Tharoor regards as having taken his religion hostage. He is defending his faith from its detractors and, at greater length, from some of its self-appointed defenders. That shared defensiveness changes how the two should be read. Neither is a neutral inquiry. Each author already knows his conclusion and is showing his working. The interesting question is whether the working holds. The unbeliever’s biography Bhagat Singh’s answer to the charge of vanity is to tell the story of how he got here, and it is a story of losing a belief slowly, not of throwing it away in a single moment of pride. He was not raised an atheist. He writes that he was brought up under the influence of his grandfather, an orthodox Arya Samajist, and later lived with his father, a firm believer who encouraged him to pray every day. As a schoolboy at the DAV school in Lahore, living in the hostel, he said his morning and evening prayers and recited the Gayatri Mantra “for hours and hours”. At the National College he began to think more freely about religion, but he was still a believer. He had begun to keep his hair long, he says, though he could never bring himself to believe in the mythology and doctrines of Sikhism or of any other religion. What moved him was the revolutionary movement, and books. The first leader he worked under, he says, could not bring himself to deny the existence of God. Another, Sachindra Nath Sanyal, sang the glory of God from the first page of his prison memoir. The four men hanged for the Kakori conspiracy spent their last days in prayer. Then came the reading: Bakunin’s God and State, something of Marx, much of Lenin and Trotsky, all of them atheists, and later a book called Common Sense by Niralamba Swami. By the end of 1926, he writes, he had become convinced that the theory of an almighty supreme being had no foundation. Then comes the part of the essay that is really his answer to the vanity charge, and the reason I trust the rest of it. After he was arrested in Lahore in May 1927, he says, police officers began urging him to pray, morning and evening. He was in exactly the position where a man might reach for God. He thought about it seriously and decided he could not make himself believe and pray. “No, I never did.” To start praying in order to be helped, he says elsewhere in the essay, would be the most selfish and degraded act a man could commit. The best argument Bhagat Singh makes against the charge of vanity is not an argument at all. It is a description of what it cost him to stay consistent. This is the heart of the essay, and it shaped how I read everything else in it. His case for atheism is not that belief is foolish. It is that he examined belief, found no reason for it, and then refused to take it up again at the one moment when it would have been most useful. Whatever one thinks of his conclusion, that is not how vanity behaves. Vanity, defined It is worth pausing on the charge itself, because Bhagat Singh takes it more seriously than his accusers did. He does not simply deny being vain. He defines the word. Vanity, he writes, “or to be more precise Ahankar, is the excess of undue pride in one’s self.” And he separates it from something that looks like it from outside: “Let me first make it clear that egotism and vanity are two different things.” The sentence that follows is the one I think the whole essay turns on: “Self-reliance is always liable to be interpreted as vanity.” That is a sharp observation, and not only about atheism. Anyone who declines a comfort that everyone around them relies on will be accused of thinking themselves above it. The person who will not pray at the funeral, the person who will not accept the consoling story, the person who insists on doing without the help that others take for granted: all of them look proud from the outside. Bhagat Singh’s claim is that what looks like pride is a decision to carry one’s own weight. Read that way, his atheism is less a metaphysical position than a moral one. The argument against God comes later in the essay. What comes first is the argument for standing on one’s own feet, and the atheism is where that argument ends up. I find it telling that the essay spends so long on the accusation of vanity and so little time being offended by it. A vain man would have been angrier. The believer’s Hinduism Tharoor’s book begins in a similar place: with himself. The first part is called “My Hinduism”, and in it he describes the faith he grew up in and why he is proud of it: chiefly, as he puts it, because it does not claim to be the only true path. But what he believes in is not quite what Bhagat Singh rejected, and this took me a while to see. The Hinduism Tharoor describes has no single founder, no single holy book and no church. There is no pope, no creed to recite, and no central authority entitled to declare someone a heretic. It is a family of traditions spread across the Vedas and the Upanishads, the epics and the Gita, the great philosophers from Adi Shankara onward, and the devotional movements. He leans heavily on a line from the Rig Veda that he returns to more than once: truth is one, and the wise call it by many names. Ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti. It functions in the book almost as a thesis statement. Everything Tharoor says about pluralism flows out of it. And he describes a religion with many paths to the divine, knowledge and devotion and action among them, and leaves the choice of path to the Hindu. He places great weight on Swami Vivekananda, and on his address to the Parliament of the World’s Religions in Chicago in 1893, where Vivekananda presented Hinduism as a religion that did not merely tolerate other faiths but accepted them as true paths. It is a distinction Tharoor keeps returning to: tolerance implies putting up with something you think is wrong, acceptance implies you think it may be right. So when Tharoor says “why I am a Hindu”, he is not really saying “why I believe what Bhagat Singh stopped believing”. He is saying something closer to “why I belong to a tradition large enough to hold people who disagree about almost everything, including God”. The hymn that doubts itself The most surprising thing in Tharoor’s book, for anyone who comes to it straight from Bhagat Singh, is how much doubt it contains. Tharoor quotes the Creation Hymn from the Rig Veda, the Nasadiya Sukta. It asks how the universe began and then declines to answer. Who really knows, it asks, and who can declare where this creation came from? The gods themselves came later than the creation. Perhaps the one who oversees it from the highest heaven knows. Or perhaps he does not know. That last line could have been written by Bhagat Singh. It is the same question he puts to believers, asked in one of the oldest texts of the religion he left, and left unanswered on purpose. Tharoor goes further. He argues that a Hindu can be astika or nastika, a believer or a denier; that one can reject the authority of the Vedas, the existence of the soul and belief in God, and still be Hindu. He is not arguing in the abstract. He describes a period of his own life in which he called himself first an atheist and then an agnostic, without ever feeling he had left the faith he was born into. It is one of the book’s boldest claims, and it has a strange consequence for my pair of books. By Tharoor’s definition, Bhagat Singh may never have left at all. The odd thing is that Bhagat Singh half-agrees about the history. His essay names Charvaka, “another independent thinker of the past ages” who “challenged the authority of God”, and points to the Buddhists and Jains as traditions that did without a creator. He simply draws the opposite conclusion: that India’s unbelievers were right, not that they were Hindus. There is something generous about a religion that says to the man who has rejected it: you are still one of us, and your doubt is part of our tradition. There is also something slippery about it. Bhagat Singh wrote his essay precisely to make his rejection unambiguous. A faith that can absorb its own apostates has made itself very hard to argue with, and a position that cannot be argued with is, from Bhagat Singh’s side of the table, not a strength. It is a way of avoiding the question. I go back and forth on this. On generous days I think Tharoor has found the most humane answer any religion has given to unbelief. On less generous days I think he has changed the subject. The question Tharoor doesn’t need to answer The core of Bhagat Singh’s essay is an old argument made with young impatience. If God is almighty, all-knowing and good, why does the world contain so much suffering? Why does He permit it? If He created the world, why did He create it like this? He does not accept that the suffering is a test, or a lesson, or a mystery beyond human understanding. He wants a straight answer and suspects there isn’t one. He puts the point with a comparison I have never been able to forget. Nero, he writes, burned one Rome and killed a limited number of people, and history has showered every venomous epithet on him for it. “Then, how are you going to justify your almighty, eternal Nero, who has been, and is still causing numberless tragedies every day, every hour and every minute?” If God made the world for his own pleasure, he asks, “where, then, is the difference between him and Nero?” It is a young man’s argument, and it has a young man’s force. It does not bother with the philosophers’ answers about free will or the greater good. It simply refuses to give the creator a moral standard lower than the one we apply to an emperor. He then turns on the theory of karma, and this is where the essay is sharpest. Suppose, he says, the suffering of this life is punishment for sins in a previous one. What kind of punishment is it? A punishment is supposed to reform the person punished. But if a man is reborn as a cow or a cat or a tree for his sins, what reformation can take place? The animal does not know what it did wrong. It cannot learn. So the punishment is not reformative, only retributive, and retribution for its own sake is exactly what civilised people are supposed to have moved beyond. And why, if God can punish sins after they happen, does He not prevent them before they happen? He brings the argument home, as he brings everything home, to politics. Why, he asks, does God not simply put a feeling into the minds of the British that would make them liberate India? And he answers himself: British rule is in India “not because God wills it, but because they possess power and we do not dare to oppose them.” God, in other words, explains nothing about the empire that guns and rifles do not explain better. Reading Tharoor with this in my head, I kept waiting for the reply, and I did not find one that would have satisfied Bhagat Singh. I do not think this is an oversight. Tharoor is not trying to prove that God exists or that God is good. His Hinduism does not stand or fall on a personal creator who could have stopped the British and chose not to. A religion whose central philosophical tradition speaks of an impersonal ultimate reality, and in which each soul is at root identical with it, is not obviously committed to the God Bhagat Singh was attacking. So in one sense the two books talk past each other. Bhagat Singh demolished a particular idea of God: personal, omnipotent, benevolent and interventionist. Tharoor defends a tradition in which that idea is one option among several. Each could claim a victory and neither would have landed a blow. But in another sense the karma argument does land, because karma is not optional in the way a personal God is. It is part of the moral architecture of the tradition Tharoor describes, and I have not been able to shake Bhagat Singh’s point about the cow. He asks what reformative effect such a punishment could possibly have: a creature reborn as a cow or a cat or a tree cannot know what it is being punished for. A system of justice in which the punished cannot understand their sentence is a strange kind of justice. On this point, as a matter of argument, I think the prisoner is right. He adds a second objection that I think is even stronger. On the karmic view, he says, poverty itself becomes a sin and a punishment. And then he asks what we would think of a criminologist, a jurist or a legislator who proposed punishments that “shall inevitably force men to commit more offences.” Poverty breeds desperation, desperation breeds wrongdoing, and wrongdoing earns a worse birth next time. A justice system that manufactures its own criminals is not a justice system. It is a trap with a theology attached. Where God comes from For a man writing against God, Bhagat Singh is surprisingly gentle about why people believe. His account of the origin of the idea is not a conspiracy. It is a description of need. God, he writes, “was brought into imaginary existence to encourage man to face boldly all the trying circumstances”. He was to be “a father, mother, sister and brother, friend and helper”, someone to turn to when a person is in great distress and has nowhere else to go. God also served, he says, as a deterrent, a watcher who keeps people from doing wrong when no one else is looking. None of this is contemptuous. It is almost tender. He understands exactly why the idea exists; he simply thinks a grown person should be able to do without it. Tharoor’s account of where the divine comes from is different in kind. In his Hinduism the idea of God is not mainly a refuge for the frightened. It is the object of a very long inquiry, carried on by philosophers who argued about whether the self and the ultimate reality are one, whether the gods themselves were created, and whether anything can be known about the beginning at all. The Creation Hymn is not the prayer of a frightened man. It is the note of a curious one. Put side by side, the two accounts do not contradict each other so much as describe two different people. Bhagat Singh describes the believer who needs God. Tharoor describes the believer who wonders about God. Both exist. The mistake is to think that either one is the only kind, and I think each author, in the end, makes that mistake about the other. What religion does in the hands of power This is where the two books, which disagree about nearly everything, agree most strongly. Bhagat Singh is careful here, more careful than his reputation. He explicitly declines to say that exploiters invented God; unlike “certain of the radicals”, he writes, he would not attribute belief to their ingenuity. But he agrees with those radicals on the essential point: that all faiths and creeds “became in turn the mere supporters of the tyrannical and exploiting institutions”. The poor are told their poverty is the fruit of their past lives and that their reward will come after death, and so they do not revolt in this one. He quotes Upton Sinclair to the effect that if you make a man believe in immortality you can rob him of everything he has, and he will help you do it. Tharoor would reject that as an account of religion in general. But a large part of his book is a case study of something very close to it. He traces the idea of Hindutva from V. D. Savarkar, who coined the term, through M. S. Golwalkar and the RSS, and he is scathing about where it has led: a political movement that treats Hinduism as a badge of national belonging rather than a spiritual path, that defines who counts as a true Indian by religion, and that has made violence respectable. He writes about the demolition of the Babri Masjid in 1992 and about the lynchings of Muslims by self-appointed protectors of the cow. He argues that these people are not defending Hinduism at all. They are using it. Put that beside Bhagat Singh and the convergence is striking. The atheist says religion, whatever its origins, has become a tool of the powerful. The believer spends a good part of his book showing, in detail and with real anger, the powerful using his religion to decide who belongs. They disagree about whether this is the essence of religion or its corruption. They agree completely about what it looks like. On this, both are right, and I find it the most useful thing either book taught me. You do not have to decide whether God exists to recognise the moment when faith is being turned into a weapon. The signs are the same from both sides: when religion is used to decide who belongs, who may be punished, and who must stay in their place. Caste This is the subject on which the two books come closest to a direct confrontation, and it is the one I expected Tharoor to handle worst. Tharoor does not defend caste. His argument is that the rigid, hereditary hierarchy is a corruption of the older idea of varna as described in the Gita, where Krishna says the fourfold order was made according to qualities and actions, not birth. On this reading the religion does not require caste, and a Hinduism true to its own texts would be free of it. His critics have said this is too easy, that inequality by birth runs through scripture, ritual and law too deeply to be explained away as a later distortion, and I think they have a point. Bhagat Singh meets the question head on, and inside his argument about karma. What, he asks, of a child born into a poor and illiterate family of “a chamar or a sweeper”? He is poor, so he cannot study; he is shunned by people who think themselves his superiors because they were born into a higher caste; and then he is told his condition is the fruit of his own past deeds. What about those who were deliberately kept ignorant by “the haughty and egotist Brahmans”? His verdict is one of the sharpest sentences in the essay: “These theories are the inventions of the privileged ones! They justify their usurped power, riches and superiority by the help of these theories.” This is where I think Tharoor is right in his conclusion and weaker in his argument. He is right that a Hinduism without caste is possible, and his own book shows that the tradition has the resources for it. But the defence that caste is a corruption rather than a feature has a limit, and Bhagat Singh finds it. When the doctrine of karma is the very thing used to explain why the sweeper deserves to be a sweeper, the corruption and the doctrine have become hard to pull apart. On caste, I read Tharoor as having made the better case for the future and Bhagat Singh as having made the better case about the past. Consolation Bhagat Singh concedes one thing to the believer, and it is a large concession. He admits that “the idea of God is helpful to man in distress”. A man who believes in God can hand his troubles over. A man facing death who believes in another life has something to look forward to. He, on the other hand, is trying, as he puts it, to stand like a man with an erect head to the last, even on the gallows. When a friend told him he would start believing in his last days, he replied that it would not happen, and that it would be an act of degradation and demoralisation on his part. He does not argue that belief brings no comfort. He argues that comfort is not a reason to believe something. His standard is harder: a man should stand on his own feet, face reality as it is, and do his duty without the promise of reward. He describes himself as a realist, and he sets out his principle in a sentence I have not been able to forget: Criticism and independent thinking are the two indispensable qualities of a revolutionary. He goes on to say that anyone who stands for progress has to criticise, disbelieve and challenge every item of the old faith. Tharoor’s book is, among other things, an answer to this in practice. His Hinduism is full of questioning, and he is proud of it: the hymn that doubts creation, the argumentative traditions of the philosophers, the absence of anyone entitled to shut an argument down. For Tharoor, faith and criticism are not opposites. He is a believer because of the kind of inquiry his tradition allows, not in spite of it. I think both of them are right, which is not the evasion it sounds like. Bhagat Singh is right that consolation is not evidence, and that a belief held because it is comforting is not really a belief, only a sedative. Tharoor is right that a tradition can contain real inquiry, and that belonging to one does not mean surrendering one’s judgement. Where they differ is in what they think inquiry is for. For Bhagat Singh it is a tool for tearing down what is false. For Tharoor it is a way of living inside a very old conversation. You need both, at different times. Two kinds of sacrifice There is one passage in Bhagat Singh’s essay that I think is the most moving thing in either book, and it is about reward. “A God-believing Hindu might be expecting to be reborn as a king,” he writes, “a Muslim or a Christian might dream of the luxuries to be enjoyed in paradise and the reward he is to get for his suffering and sacrifices. But, what am I to expect?” He knows the answer: when the rope is fitted round his neck and the rafters are removed from under his feet, “that will be the final moment”. Nothing further. And so: “With no selfish motive or desire to be awarded here or hereafter, quite disinterestedly, have I devoted my life to the cause of independence.” The argument is subtle and I think it is right. A sacrifice made in expectation of reward is still, in part, a transaction. The believer who dies for his country and expects paradise has made a very good bargain. The unbeliever who dies for it expects nothing, and so his sacrifice is, in the strictest sense, a gift. Bhagat Singh is not claiming to be braver than the believers who went to the gallows before him. He is claiming that his account of why he is going is cleaner. Here is the irony, and I think Tharoor would enjoy it. The ideal Bhagat Singh describes, doing one’s duty with no desire for its fruits, is the ideal of the Gita, the text Tharoor leans on to argue that caste was meant to follow qualities and actions rather than birth. The atheist in his cell, refusing the reward of heaven, is living the Gita’s teaching more strictly than the believers he describes, who are counting on theirs. Bhagat Singh would not have thanked anyone for pointing this out. But it suggests that the line between the two books runs less between belief and unbelief than between those who do their duty for a reward and those who do it for nothing. The atheist in his cell, refusing the reward of heaven, is living the Gita’s teaching more strictly than the believers he describes. Can a republic stand on a religion? The last part of Tharoor’s book is called “Taking Back Hinduism”, and its argument is political. India’s secular democracy, he contends, is not something imposed on Hinduism from outside. It grows out of Hinduism’s own diversity and its acceptance of many paths. A religion that never needed one book, one prophet or one church is, on this view, the natural soil for a republic that does not need one faith. It is an attractive argument and a strategically clever one. If secularism is presented as an alien import, it is easy for Hindutva to attack it as a betrayal of the majority. If it is presented as the majority’s own inheritance, the attack becomes much harder. Bhagat Singh would have seen the danger in it straight away. A freedom that rests on the generosity of the majority’s religion is only as secure as the majority’s reading of that religion. Tharoor’s own book shows how quickly that reading can change: the second part is a long account of a political movement persuading millions of Hindus that their faith requires something quite different from acceptance. If the republic’s floor is made of Hinduism’s tolerance, then whoever wins the argument about Hinduism gets to decide how solid the floor is. Bhagat Singh’s alternative is to build the floor out of something else: criticism, independent thinking, and the refusal to let any belief, however old, go unexamined. That foundation cannot be captured by winning an argument about scripture, because it does not depend on scripture. But it has its own weakness, and Tharoor’s approach is the answer to it. A republic founded on reason alone, and seen by the majority as hostile to their faith, will not keep the majority’s loyalty for long. People do not defend institutions they believe despise them. I have come to think the two arguments need each other. A secular state needs a floor that does not depend on anyone’s theology, which is Bhagat Singh’s point. And it needs the majority to feel that the floor belongs to them too, which is Tharoor’s. The first without the second is brittle. The second without the first is a gift that can be withdrawn. Where each of them goes wrong It would be too neat to leave it there, and both books have a blind spot that the other makes visible. Bhagat Singh’s is in his contempt for prayer. He calls praying for help the most selfish and degraded thing a man can do, and he means all prayer. But Tharoor’s book, and the tradition it describes, is full of devotion that asks for nothing: the bhakti poets, the philosopher who spends his life on the nature of reality, the hymn that asks whether even the creator knows how creation began. Bhagat Singh was right about the prayer that bargains. He had no room for the prayer that only wonders, and the Creation Hymn is that kind of prayer. Tharoor’s blind spot is the mirror image. He spends much of the book distinguishing true Hinduism, tolerant, plural and accepting, from the Hindutva that he says has hijacked it. I agree with nearly everything he says about Hindutva. But the move itself, declaring that the real religion is the one I recognise and the people I disagree with are not really practising it, is exactly the move he objects to when Hindutva makes it. A religion with no pope, as he rightly says, has nobody to decide who the real Hindus are. That cuts both ways. The mistakes have the same shape. Each man looks at a religion that has been many things to many people over thousands of years, and chooses the version that suits his argument. Bhagat Singh sees the religion of the privileged and of the bargain. Tharoor sees the religion of the sages and of acceptance. Both versions are real. Neither is the whole thing. What I kept I did not end up where either of them did, which is probably the point of reading them together. From Bhagat Singh I have kept a test. When I notice that I believe something, I ask whether I would still believe it if it stopped being comfortable, and whether I would still hold it in the one situation where giving it up would make my life easier. He applied that test to God in a police lock-up in 1927 and did not blink. Most of my beliefs have never been tested half that hard. From Tharoor I have kept the Creation Hymn, and the idea behind it. It seems to me the most honest thing ever written about the origin of things: a text at the root of a religious tradition that asks the biggest question it can and then admits that perhaps even the one who knows does not know. If that is where a faith begins, it has at least begun in the right place. And from the two of them together I have kept the thing they agree on, which is the thing I trust most because they agree on it from opposite sides. Whatever you believe about God, watch what people do with the belief. When it is used to decide who belongs, who deserves to suffer, and who should stay where they are, it has stopped being about God, and both the believer and the unbeliever should say so. Both books begin with the same three words. I have come to think that “why I am” is not a question you answer once. It is one you have to keep answering, and a good answer is one that still holds up when someone as honest as a prisoner, or as well-read as a politician, asks you again.
three-ways-to-count-a-people: Today is the fifteenth of August, India’s Independence Day. I live in Geneva, a city that became Swiss by choice in 1815 and still votes on something every few months, and two weeks ago Switzerland celebrated its own national day. This summer was so hot and dry that the fireworks were called off for fear of fires, and Lake Geneva got light shows instead. I spent that day, the first of August, on the Fronalpstock, above Stoos in the canton of Schwyz, walking the ridge and listening to alphorns. From the summit you look down on Lake Lucerne and across the water to the Rütli, the meadow where, by tradition, men from three valleys swore the oath that the first of August commemorates. Schwyz gave the country its name. It is a good place to think about what it means for people to decide things together. In November the United States, where I also lived for a while, will hold its midterm elections on a Tuesday chosen in 1845 for the convenience of farmers. I have lived under three very different answers to the same question: how do you turn what millions of people want into a law? India answers it by asking almost a billion adults to choose a representative, once every five years, in a single enormous event. The United States answers it through a layered machine of states, districts and electors, designed by men who distrusted the very majority they were empowering. Switzerland answers it by asking its citizens directly, several times a year, about specific laws, and treating parliament as one voice among several. I want to look at the three side by side: where each system came from, what it assumes about the people it serves, why it works where it works and fails where it fails, and what it has done to women, who in each of the three were the largest group to be left out and, in different ways, still are. I am not going to propose fixes. Every country that has tried to import another’s electoral system has discovered that the system was the least transferable part of the arrangement. What I want to understand is why each one fits its country, and where the fit pinches. Plate 1 Three flags tied in one knot, and three different ways of counting the people under them. What I am comparing A brief map, and then I will try not to get lost in it. India elects the Lok Sabha, the lower house of Parliament, in 543 single-member constituencies. Whoever gets the most votes in a constituency wins it, even without a majority: the system known as first past the post. The party or coalition that controls the Lok Sabha forms the government. The upper house, the Rajya Sabha, is elected indirectly by the state legislatures. An independent Election Commission runs the whole thing, nationally. The United States elects a House of Representatives of 435 members, also by first past the post in single-member districts, and a Senate of 100, two per state regardless of population. The president is chosen separately, through an Electoral College in which each state’s weight is its number of representatives plus its two senators. There is no national election authority. Elections are run by the states, and in practice by thousands of counties and towns. Switzerland elects a National Council of 200 members by proportional representation, canton by canton, and a Council of States of 46, two for most cantons. Parliament then elects a seven-member Federal Council that governs collectively; there is no prime minister and no president in any strong sense. But the defining feature is that the people are a legislature too. Any law parliament passes can be challenged by 50,000 signatures and sent to a national vote. Any 100,000 citizens can propose a change to the constitution and force a vote on it. Every constitutional amendment must be approved by a majority of voters and a majority of cantons. That is the machinery. The interesting part is why it looks like this. India: everyone at once The most radical decision in the history of Indian democracy was made before the first vote was cast. The Constitution that came into force on 26 January 1950 gave the vote to every adult, man or woman, rich or poor, literate or not, on the same day. There was no ladder: no property qualification to be lowered decade by decade, no literacy test, no staged extension of the franchise. The country went, in a single step, from a colonial electorate of a propertied minority to universal adult suffrage. It is hard to overstate how reckless this looked at the time. The census of 1951 found that about 18 per cent of Indians could read. For women the figure was under 9 per cent. The first general election, held over four months from October 1951 to early 1952, asked about 173 million people, most of them poor and most of them unable to read a ballot, to choose a government. Turnout was about 45 per cent. The man who made it work was Sukumar Sen, a civil servant appointed as the first Chief Election Commissioner in 1950. Because most voters could not read names, each party was given a picture: a pair of bullocks, a hut, a lamp. At first each candidate had a separate ballot box marked with their symbol, so that a voter could put the paper in the box with the right picture. More than 224,000 polling booths were set up. It was, at the time, the largest election ever held, and it was held in a country that had been partitioned in bloodshed four years earlier. The choice of first past the post was less radical. It was the system the British had used and the one India’s political class knew. What India added to it was a set of guarantees for the people most likely to be shut out: constituencies reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, in which only candidates from those communities may stand, although everyone in the constituency votes. Today 84 Lok Sabha seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and 47 for Scheduled Tribes. Since a Supreme Court ruling in 2013, every Indian voting machine has carried one more button after the candidates: NOTA, “None of the Above”. It cannot win; if NOTA gets the most votes, the candidate in second place is still elected. But it lets a voter walk all the way to the booth, in the heat, and say formally that nobody on the list deserves the vote. I find it one of the more honest features of any ballot I know. The man who understood best what all this could and could not do was B. R. Ambedkar, who chaired the committee that drafted the Constitution. In his last speech to the Constituent Assembly, on 25 November 1949, he warned: On the 26th of January 1950, we are going to enter into a life of contradictions. In politics we will have equality and in social and economic life we will have inequality. In politics we will be recognizing the principle of one man one vote and one vote one value. In our social and economic life, we shall, by reason of our social and economic structure, continue to deny the principle of one man one value. That paragraph is the key to Indian democracy. The founders did not give the poor the vote because the country was ready for it. They gave it because they believed the vote was the one lever the poor could pull against a society that was not ready at all. In the Gir forest in Gujarat, the Election Commission sets up a polling booth for one man. For years it was a priest named Bharatdas Bapu, the only resident of a temple deep in lion country; since his death in 2019 it has been his successor. A team of officials and security guards walks in, sets up a voting machine for a single voter, and reports a turnout of one hundred per cent. It is the most Indian thing I know about Indian elections: the absurd, stubborn insistence that nobody is too remote to be asked. The United States: a machine built to check the majority The American system was designed by people with the opposite anxiety. India’s founders feared that ordinary people would be excluded. America’s founders, in Philadelphia in 1787, feared what ordinary people might do if they were not. Almost every oddity of the American system is a compromise between competing fears. The small states feared domination by the large ones, so they got a Senate in which every state has two seats regardless of size. Some delegates feared a president chosen directly by an excitable national majority; others feared one chosen by Congress and beholden to it. The Electoral College was the compromise: each state would choose electors, in whatever way it liked, and the electors would choose the president. The slave-holding states wanted their enslaved populations counted for representation without granting those people any rights, and the Constitution’s three-fifths clause counted each enslaved person as three-fifths of a person when apportioning seats in the House, and therefore votes in the Electoral College. The result was not a democracy in the modern sense. Senators were chosen by state legislatures until the Seventeenth Amendment introduced direct election in 1913. The right to vote was left to the states, which restricted it by property, race and sex. The story of the American franchise is a story of amendments prying it open one group at a time: the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870, forbidding denial of the vote by race, which the Southern states then nullified in practice for nearly a century; the Nineteenth in 1920, for women; the Twenty-fourth in 1964, abolishing poll taxes in federal elections; the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which finally put federal force behind the Fifteenth; the Twenty-sixth in 1971, lowering the voting age to eighteen. That history explains why the American system has no single owner. There are more than 10,000 election jurisdictions in the United States, some with a few hundred voters and the largest with more than five million. The rules on who may register, how, when and where to vote, and how votes are counted differ from state to state and often from county to county. Congressional districts are redrawn every ten years, mostly by state legislatures, which means that in many states the politicians draw the lines of their own contests. In 2019, in Rucho v. Common Cause, the Supreme Court held that partisan gerrymandering, however “incompatible with democratic principles”, was a political question outside the reach of federal courts. Six years earlier, in Shelby County v. Holder, it had struck down the formula that decided which jurisdictions, mostly in the South, had to get federal approval before changing their voting rules. The size of the House has been frozen at 435 since the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929, although the population has nearly tripled since. The Senate’s structure means that California, with nearly forty million people, has the same two senators as Wyoming, with fewer than six hundred thousand. And five times, in 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000 and 2016, the person who became president did not win the most votes. Why a Tuesday in November? A law of 1845 fixed the date for a country of farmers. November came after the harvest and before the roads froze. Sunday was for church, and Wednesday was market day in many places, so a voter who might need a day to reach the county seat could leave on Monday and vote on Tuesday. The farmers are long gone. The Tuesday remains, a working day on which millions of people have to fit voting around their jobs. Switzerland: the people as a chamber of parliament Switzerland’s system was built out of a different fear again: the fear of being ruled from above at all. The modern federal state dates from 1848, after a short civil war in 1847 between Catholic and Protestant cantons. The new constitution created a federal government but kept most power in the cantons, and the cantons themselves had long traditions of self-government, some of them including the Landsgemeinde, the open-air assembly at which the citizens of a canton gather in the town square once a year and decide its laws by a show of hands. Two cantons, Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden, still govern themselves that way. Direct democracy at the federal level came in stages. In 1874 a revised constitution introduced the optional referendum: if enough citizens object to a law parliament has passed, it goes to a popular vote. Today that takes 50,000 signatures collected within 100 days. In 1891 came the popular initiative, which lets citizens propose an amendment to the constitution: 100,000 signatures in 18 months, and the country must vote on it. Proportional representation for the National Council followed in 1919, after a popular initiative forced it through. The Swiss government counts roughly 240 popular initiatives that have gone to the vote since 1891. About two dozen have passed. That low success rate is misleading, because the initiative’s real power lies elsewhere: parliament, knowing a vote is coming, often drafts a counter-proposal that takes some of the initiative’s demands and passes that instead. The optional referendum works the same way in reverse. Because almost any law can be challenged, the parties that write laws have an incentive to include anyone who could collect 50,000 signatures against them. This is the origin of the most distinctive feature of Swiss government: concordance. From 1959 to 2003, the seven seats on the Federal Council were shared among the four largest parties by a fixed arrangement known as the magic formula: two, two, two and one. There is no government and opposition in the British or Indian sense. Everyone large enough to cause trouble through a referendum is brought inside. The result is a government that almost never changes and a people that constantly overrules it. Today about 5.6 million Swiss citizens can vote. They are called to the polls about four times a year, and more than nine in ten of them now vote by post, from the kitchen table, weeks before the official day. At the Landsgemeinde in Appenzell Innerrhoden, a man could traditionally prove his right to vote by showing his sword. Many still do; the others, and every woman, show a voting card. The swords are a reminder of what the vote originally was in these valleys: the right of the men who could defend the community to decide its affairs. It took until 1990, and a ruling from the country’s highest court, for that definition to include the women standing in the same square. Scale, and what it permits The most obvious difference between the three systems is size, and I think it explains more than any other single factor. In 2024 India had about 978 million registered voters. The election was held in seven phases between April and June. There were about 10.5 lakh, or 1.05 million, polling stations, staffed by roughly 15 million officials, with more than 5.5 million electronic voting machines. About 65.8 per cent of voters turned out, well over 600 million people. Machines have been used in every constituency since 2004, partly because counting paper ballots on this scale took days and invited fraud. The one thing every Indian voter comes home with is a purple-black mark on the left index finger. The ink, made to be impossible to wash off for weeks, has been supplied for every general election since 1962 by a single state-owned company, Mysore Paints and Varnish, which now exports it to more than thirty countries. It is the cheapest anti-fraud device in the democratic world, and the most photographed: every election, a billion people’s feed fills with the same raised finger. The United States had around 245 million eligible voters in 2024, and about 64 per cent of them voted, the second-highest turnout in more than a century, after 2020. Switzerland’s entire electorate is smaller than the number of voters in several Indian states. Scale determines what is possible. In the past few years Switzerland has asked its citizens about the purchase of fighter jets, the rules on hunting wolves, a thirteenth monthly pension payment and the widening of motorways, and it can do so because the whole country is smaller than the city of Delhi and its voters are among the most educated and best informed in the world. Every household receives an official booklet setting out the arguments for and against each proposal. The machinery is cheap enough, and the voters are close enough to the issues, that asking them directly is feasible. India cannot do this, and not only for logistical reasons. The Indian election is a single enormous act of consent, repeated every five years, in which the people choose who will govern them and then, for the most part, let them. It is closer to hiring a government than to co-writing its laws. That is not a defect. It is the only form of democracy that could possibly operate at the scale of a billion people in a country with the literacy India had in 1951. The genius of the Indian system has always been logistics, not deliberation: the ability to put a voting machine within a couple of kilometres of almost every voter in the country and get the results counted in a day. The United States sits in between, and the American system is the one most clearly strained by its size. Its structure was designed for thirteen states and about four million people. It now serves 50 states and over 330 million. Features that were modest compromises at the founding, like the equal representation of states in the Senate or a House whose size was fixed a century ago, have grown into large distortions simply because the country grew around them. The genius of the Indian system has always been logistics, not deliberation. Why they work It is fashionable to talk about all three democracies as being in crisis. I want to start with the ways in which each of them works, because each one does something the other two cannot. India’s works because it includes. The most remarkable fact about Indian elections is who votes. In most Western democracies, the rich vote more than the poor and the educated more than the uneducated. In India it has often been the other way round. The political scientist Yogendra Yadav described a “second democratic upsurge” from the late 1980s onward, in which lower castes, poorer and rural voters entered politics in large numbers and began to turn out at rates matching or exceeding those of urban, upper-caste voters. For a great many Indians the vote is the one moment when the state treats them as equal to everyone else, and they use it. It also works because it can throw governments out. Since 1977, when the voters removed Indira Gandhi’s government after the Emergency, Indian elections have repeatedly defeated incumbents at the national and state levels, and the losers have left office. That is not a small thing in the region India sits in. America’s works because it is hard to capture. The fragmentation that makes American elections so confusing also makes them resilient. No single official, no single agency and no single party controls how Americans vote. After the 2020 election, when the outgoing president tried to overturn the result, the effort ran into thousands of local officials of both parties, state courts and state legislatures that refused to go along. A centralised system would have had one point of failure. The American system has ten thousand, which also means it has ten thousand points of resistance. Switzerland’s works because it forces agreement. A government that knows any law can be put to a national vote cannot afford to legislate for its own supporters alone. Concordance, the permanent sharing of power among all the major parties, is not a cultural quirk of the Swiss. It is a rational response to the referendum. The result is policy that changes slowly and rarely swings, and a government that very few citizens see as illegitimate, because they can always overrule it. Why they fail Each system’s failures are the side effects of its strengths. India’s inclusion comes with distortion. First past the post rewards the largest party far beyond its share of the vote. In 2014 the BJP won about 31 per cent of the national vote and 282 seats, an outright majority of the Lok Sabha. In 2019 it won about 37 per cent and 303 seats. In 2024 it won a similar share, about 36.6 per cent, and only 240 seats, because the opposition consolidated. The same vote share produced very different outcomes depending on how opponents arranged themselves. That is not unique to India, but in a country this diverse it means that a party can govern alone with the support of little more than a third of voters. The system has also become extraordinarily expensive to enter. The Association for Democratic Reforms found that 93 per cent of the MPs elected in 2024 were crorepatis, declaring assets of more than ten million rupees, in a country where most people earn a small fraction of that. It also found that 251 of the 543 winners, 46 per cent, had declared criminal cases against themselves, up from 30 per cent in 2009. The poorest voters turn out in the largest numbers to choose among candidates who are overwhelmingly rich, and often under investigation. America’s resilience comes with paralysis and minority rule. The same structure that makes the system hard to capture makes it hard to govern through. A party can win the presidency without the most votes, control the Senate on behalf of a minority of the population, and draw House districts that entrench its position. First past the post in single-member districts also produces a two-party system, as political scientists have long observed it tends to, and in a country as large and varied as the United States, two parties must each contain coalitions so broad that they barely cohere. The fragmentation of election administration means that the experience of voting, how long the queue is, which identification you need, how early you can vote, depends heavily on where you live. Switzerland’s consensus comes with exclusion and slow motion. The first problem is who takes part. Average turnout in federal votes over the past few years has been just under 50 per cent, which means that a typical national decision is made by about a quarter of the citizens. And the citizens are not the whole population: about 27 per cent of the nine million people living in Switzerland do not hold a Swiss passport and cannot vote at the federal level at all, although some cantons and communes, including Geneva’s communes after eight years of residence, let them vote locally. A country that prides itself on asking the people asks only some of them. One canton has taken a different view of low turnout. Schaffhausen is the only canton where voting is compulsory: a citizen who does not vote pays a fine, doubled in 2014 to six francs. It is less a punishment than a reminder, and it works. Turnout in Schaffhausen runs well above the national average; in the 2014 immigration vote it was about 70 per cent against a national 56. The second problem is what a majority can do to a minority. In 2009, 57.5 per cent of voters approved a constitutional ban on building new minarets, in a country where Muslims had no say in the matter and very few minarets existed. In 2014 an initiative “against mass immigration” passed by 50.3 per cent, a margin of about 19,500 votes, and put the country’s agreement on free movement with the European Union in question. Direct democracy is excellent at expressing what the median voter wants. It has no built-in protection for those the median voter does not like. The third problem is speed, and it is the one that matters most for the rest of this essay. When every major change needs a popular majority, change arrives only when the majority is ready for it. Sometimes that is a virtue. Sometimes it means that the rights of half the population wait for the other half to approve them. Trusting the count A vote is only as good as the belief that it was counted. Each of the three countries has had to earn that belief in its own way, and each has a different weak point. India counts faster than anyone. On 4 June 2024, the votes of more than 600 million people were counted in a single day, and by evening the country knew the result. That is possible only because the ballots are electronic. The machines have been challenged repeatedly, and every major party has at some point, usually after losing, suggested that they could be tampered with. Since 2019 every machine has been paired with a printer, the VVPAT, first tried in 2013, that shows the voter a paper slip of their choice, so that a sample of paper records can be checked against the electronic count. In April 2024 the Supreme Court rejected a petition to go back to paper ballots or to count every paper slip, and warned against “baseless apprehensions” about the Election Commission. India’s trust in the count rests on the Commission itself, an institution that has been accused of many things but, for most of its history, has been widely believed to count honestly. Switzerland’s trust rests on paper and on habit. Almost everyone votes by post, and the counting is done by local officials, often volunteers, in each commune. Results arrive on the Sunday afternoon of the vote. When Switzerland tried to move to online voting, it tested the system in public: in 2019 it invited hackers from around the world to attack the Swiss Post e-voting system, and researchers found serious flaws in the source code. The government stopped the trials. They restarted in 2023 in three cantons, for a small number of voters, mostly Swiss living abroad. A country that votes four times a year decided it would rather be slow and certain than fast and doubtful. The United States has the hardest version of the problem, because it has no single counter. Each state counts in its own way and at its own speed, and several do not begin processing postal ballots until election day. In 2020 it took four days before the major news organisations could call the presidential result. The losing candidate then claimed the election had been stolen, and his campaign and its allies filed dozens of lawsuits, which failed almost without exception, many of them in front of judges he had appointed. The count held. But trust in it, among a large part of the country, did not recover, and the American system has no single institution with the standing to settle the question the way the Indian Election Commission or the Swiss communes do. What strikes me is that trust in the count does not track the technology. India trusts machines, Switzerland trusts paper and post, and the United States uses both, yet it is the United States where doubt has done the most damage. The count is a technical problem. Trust in it is a political one. What it costs, and who pays Elections cost money, and the question of whose money shapes a system as much as any rule about ballots. The two largest are also the two most expensive in the world. The Centre for Media Studies estimated that the 2024 Indian general election cost about 1.35 lakh crore rupees in total, parties, candidates and the state together, more than double its estimate for 2019. OpenSecrets estimated that the 2024 federal election cycle in the United States cost about 15.9 billion dollars, also a record. In both countries most of that money is spent by parties and candidates, and in both the question of where it comes from is only partly answered. India’s electoral bond scheme, which allowed anonymous donations to parties through banks, was struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2024. In the United States, since the Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision of 2010, outside groups can spend without limit on political advertising. The consequence for the voter is visible in who stands. When 93 per cent of Indian MPs are crorepatis, the first filter on who represents a billion people is not the voter but the cost of entry. Switzerland had, until very recently, almost no rules at all. For most of its history there was no requirement to disclose who funded parties or referendum campaigns, which is striking in a country where campaigns on specific laws are constant and where a well-funded campaign can shape the outcome of a vote. Federal transparency rules came into force only on 23 October 2022: campaigns spending more than 50,000 francs must disclose their finances, and donors giving more than 15,000 francs must be named. In direct democracy, where citizens decide laws themselves, the question of who pays for persuading them matters even more than in a representative system. It is one of the odder facts about the most democratic country in Europe that it took until 2022 to ask it. What makes a system fit Why did these three countries end up with these three systems, and why do the systems more or less hold? I think five factors matter more than any design choice. Development. India chose a system that asked the least of each voter, one choice every five years, marked with a symbol, because in 1951 it could not ask for more. Switzerland chose a system that asks a great deal of each voter, dozens of decisions a year on detailed questions, and it can do so because its citizens are wealthy, highly educated and have the time to read the booklet. The American system asks something in between, but it asks it unevenly, which is why turnout there still tracks income and education in a way it does not in India. Culture. Each system encodes a founding memory. India’s encodes the memory of exclusion: a colonial state in which Indians had no say, and a social order in which most Indians had no standing, so the founders put everyone in at once. America’s encodes the memory of a distant king and the fear of any power, including a popular majority, that could act without restraint, so the founders divided power until it could barely move. Switzerland’s encodes the memory of village and valley self-government and the suspicion of anyone who claims to decide on the citizens’ behalf, so the Swiss kept the right to decide for themselves. Social divides. Every one of these countries is divided, and each system is shaped around its divisions. India’s deepest divides are caste, religion and language, and its answer was reserved constituencies and a federal structure built partly along linguistic lines. America’s deepest divide was race, and for most of its history its electoral system was built to preserve that division rather than bridge it; much of the twentieth-century history of American voting is the story of dismantling what the nineteenth century built. Switzerland’s divides are language and religion: German, French, Italian and Romansh; Catholic and Protestant. Its answer was proportional representation and concordance, so that no language group and no confession could simply be outvoted in government. The famous “Röstigraben”, the divide between German- and French-speaking Switzerland, still shows up in referendum results, most memorably in 1992, when the country rejected joining the European Economic Area by 50.3 per cent, with the French-speaking cantons voting largely in favour and the German-speaking ones against. Climate and geography. This sounds trivial and is not. The American election date was set by the agricultural calendar. The Indian election is shaped by heat and monsoon: it is usually held in spring, before the rains, across weeks rather than days, because security forces and officials have to move across a subcontinent. In 2024, the final phase was held on 1 June, in a heatwave, and dozens of polling staff died of heatstroke; in Uttar Pradesh alone the state’s chief electoral officer reported 33 deaths on the last day of voting. Switzerland’s direct democracy grew in small Alpine communities where people could physically gather in one place, and the Landsgemeinden that survive are held outdoors in spring. Geography made Swiss democracy intimate and Indian democracy heroic. International position. Each system also reflects where the country stands in the world. India’s democracy was, from the start, a claim made to the world: that a poor, newly independent, enormously diverse country could govern itself by consent. That claim has been one of India’s main sources of standing ever since. The United States, as a superpower, has discovered that its elections are of interest to everyone, including hostile governments, and the question of foreign interference has become part of its domestic politics. Switzerland’s neutrality and its refusal to join the European Union are expressed and defended through the referendum: its relationship with Europe has been set, again and again, by popular votes, which gives the Swiss people a direct say over foreign policy that citizens of almost no other country have. Who else is left out Women are the largest group each of these systems once excluded, and I will come to them. But every system draws a line somewhere, and where it draws the line tells you what it believes a voter is. Prisoners. India bars everyone in prison from voting, convicted or not. Section 62(5) of the Representation of the People Act applies equally to someone serving a sentence and to someone who has been arrested and is waiting, sometimes for years, for a trial; more than four lakh undertrial prisoners could not vote in 2024. Yet a person facing criminal charges can stand for Parliament, and nearly half of the current Lok Sabha does. In India, it is easier to be a candidate with a criminal case against you than a voter behind bars. The United States leaves the question to the states, and 48 of them take the vote away from people with felony convictions in some form, some only while they are in prison, some for much longer. The Sentencing Project estimated that about four million Americans could not vote in 2024 because of a felony conviction. Only Maine and Vermont, along with the District of Columbia, let people vote from prison. Switzerland does neither. Being in prison does not affect a Swiss citizen’s right to vote. Emigrants. This is the line that touches me personally. An Indian citizen living abroad can register to vote, but can vote only in person, at the polling station in their home constituency, with their passport. There is no postal vote for overseas Indians. An Indian living in Geneva who wants to vote in a general election has to be in India on the day. The Swiss abroad vote by post, and a few cantons now let some of them vote online. Of about 800,000 Swiss citizens living abroad, a little over 220,000 are registered. Americans abroad have been able to vote absentee by federal law since 1986. Residents who are not citizens. Switzerland’s case I have described: about a quarter of the people who live here have no federal vote. India and the United States draw the same line, citizenship, but because far fewer of their residents are foreigners, it excludes proportionally far fewer people. Glarus, one of the two cantons that still govern themselves in the town square, did something no other Swiss canton has done. At its Landsgemeinde in 2007, the citizens voted by show of hands to lower the cantonal voting age to sixteen. The oldest form of democracy in the country produced its most youthful electorate. Put together, these lines say something about each system’s idea of a voter. India’s is a person who is physically present: in the constituency, at the booth, out of prison, with a mark on their finger. Switzerland’s is a member of a community of citizens, wherever they are and whatever they have done, but only a member. America’s is whatever each state decides it should be. Each definition leaves out a different group of people, and none of them leaves out nobody. The women Every one of these systems was designed by men, and in each of them women were the largest group of people to whom the promise of the vote did not, at first, apply. What happened next differs sharply, and the differences say a great deal about the systems themselves. India: the vote first, the power much later Indian women did not have to fight for the vote in the way that American and Swiss women did. Some had it in limited form under British rule: in 1921 the Madras Presidency became the first province to let women vote, on the same property and education qualifications as men, which in practice meant very few of them. The Constitution then gave every adult woman the vote at the same moment as every adult man. In 1951, most of the women who were enfranchised could not read. That early gift has not translated into power, and it has taken decades even to translate into participation. In 1962 women’s turnout was about 47 per cent, far below men’s. By 2014 it had risen to about 66 per cent. In 2019, for the first time in a general election, women voted at a slightly higher rate than men, and in 2024 they did so again: 65.78 per cent against 65.55 per cent. And yet the rolls have been missing women. Prannoy Roy and Dorab Sopariwala estimated in their book The Verdict that about 21 million eligible Indian women were not registered to vote in 2019, roughly the entire electorate of a state like Jharkhand. Women who marry and move to their husband’s village, as many rural Indian women do, often fall off one roll without being added to another. In Parliament, the change has barely happened. The 2024 Lok Sabha has 74 women, 13.6 per cent of its members, fewer than the 78 elected in 2019. Fewer than one in ten candidates was a woman. Parties, which choose candidates, have simply not chosen them. India has tried to force the issue through quotas. The 73rd and 74th Amendments of the early 1990s reserved one-third of seats in village councils and municipal bodies for women, and millions of women have since been elected to local office. But the reform brought with it a phenomenon so common that it has its own name: the sarpanch pati, the “sarpanch’s husband”, who runs the village council while his wife holds the title. In 2023 Parliament passed the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserving a third of the seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women. It will take effect only after the next census and a redrawing of constituencies, which means the women it promises are, at the earliest, a general election away. India gave women the vote before it gave them literacy, and the vote before it gave them power. The system includes them as voters as fully as it includes anyone. It has barely begun to include them as representatives. The United States: a century of fighting, a ceiling still in place American women fought for the vote for more than seventy years. The first women’s rights convention met at Seneca Falls in 1848. The territory of Wyoming gave women the vote in 1869, partly as a way to attract settlers and publicity. Montana elected Jeannette Rankin to Congress in 1916, four years before most American women could vote for her. The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. But the Nineteenth Amendment did not reach everyone it described. In the Southern states, Black women were kept from voting by the same poll taxes, literacy tests and violence that kept Black men from voting, and they were not effectively enfranchised until the Voting Rights Act of 1965. For many American women the date that matters is not 1920 but 1965. Since then, women have become the more reliable voters. In every presidential election since 1980, a higher proportion of eligible women than eligible men has voted, and there are now millions more women registered than men. Representation has lagged far behind. The 119th Congress has 155 women, 26 senators and 129 representatives, a record, and still only about 28 per cent of its voting members. The United States has never had a woman president. In 2016 a woman won the popular vote and lost the Electoral College. The Equal Rights Amendment, which would have written sex equality into the Constitution, passed Congress in 1972 and failed to be ratified by the necessary 38 states before its deadline in 1982. The American system gave women the vote through the same slow, amendment-by-amendment process through which it gave everyone else the vote, and it has kept them out of its highest office through the same winner-take-all structure that shapes everything else about it. Switzerland: the men decided Switzerland is the country I live in, and its record is the one I find hardest to explain to people who know it only as the model democracy. Swiss women could not vote in federal elections until 1971. On 1 February 1959, the men of Switzerland voted on whether to give women the vote, and 67 per cent of them said no. Some cantons moved first: Vaud and Neuchâtel gave women the vote at cantonal level in 1959, and Geneva, the city I am writing from, on 6 March 1960. At the federal level, it took until 7 February 1971, when 65.7 per cent of the male electorate voted yes. Even then, the cantons could keep their own rules. Appenzell Ausserrhoden let women vote in cantonal matters only in 1989. Appenzell Innerrhoden refused to do so at all, and its men went on voting in the town square by show of hands. On 27 November 1990 the Federal Supreme Court ruled that the canton was violating the federal constitution, and women voted at its Landsgemeinde for the first time in the spring of 1991. This is where direct democracy’s structural weakness becomes most visible. In a representative system, a parliament can extend the vote to a group that does not yet have it. In the Swiss system, the question of whether women should vote was put, repeatedly, to the men who already could, and the men could say no. The people as a legislature meant, for a very long time, the men as a legislature. The same institution that makes Swiss democracy so legitimate in the eyes of those inside it made it unusually hard for those outside it to get in. Swiss women have not forgotten. On 14 June 1991, twenty years after federal suffrage, around half a million women took part in a national strike, the largest public mobilisation in the country since the general strike of 1918. On 14 June 2019 they did it again, with a similar number, demanding equal pay, recognition of unpaid work and more representation. And here is the paradox that runs through all three countries. In the 2019 federal election, women won 42 per cent of the seats in the National Council. In 2023 that fell to 38.5 per cent. Switzerland, which enfranchised women last, has by far the highest share of women in its lower house of the three. India, which enfranchised them first, has the lowest. The order in which each country gave women the vote is the exact reverse of the order in which women now sit in its parliament. India first, and 13.6 per cent. The United States in the middle, and about 28 per cent. Switzerland last, and 38.5 per cent. I have not found a single explanation for this that satisfies me, and I have come to suspect that the right answer is that the vote was never the main obstacle. What each system does to women follows its general logic. India’s system includes everyone as a voter and lets parties decide who governs; the parties have decided that governing is mostly a job for men. America’s system includes people slowly, through struggle, and its winner-take-all offices, above all the presidency, remain the hardest to reach. Switzerland’s system, where the people decide directly, excluded women for as long as the voting majority wanted it to, and then, once they were in, proportional representation gave parties an incentive to put women on their lists, and voters an easy way to choose them. What the three have in common Put the three side by side and the differences are so large that it is tempting to say they have nothing in common. I think they have one thing, and it is the most important thing about each of them. Each system is built around a fear, and each system’s failures are the side effects of guarding against that fear. India feared exclusion, the exclusion of the poor, the illiterate and the low-caste from a state that had always ignored them. So it put everyone in at once and built an enormous, efficient machine to ask them all. The price is a system that asks people very little between elections, rewards whoever can assemble the largest coalition, and has become the preserve of the rich, while the poor turn out in their hundreds of millions to choose among them. America feared tyranny, of a king, of a central government, and of a majority. So it divided power until no one could easily seize it. The price is a system in which a minority can win, in which the lines of districts are drawn by those who run in them, and in which the right to vote has had to be won group by group against the resistance of the structure itself. Switzerland feared being governed from above. So it kept the final say for the citizens themselves. The price is a system in which the citizens can refuse to share that say with anyone else: with the quarter of the population who are not citizens, and, for most of the twentieth century, with women. I said at the start that I would not propose fixes, and I will keep to that. But I have come to think that the most useful question to ask of any electoral system is not whether it is democratic. All three of these are, in their different ways. The useful question is: who is it protecting, and from what? The answer tells you both why the system works and whom it will leave out. On the evidence of the three countries I have lived in, the people each system was designed to protect have usually been well protected. The people it was not designed for have had to fight their way in, and in all three, for a very long time, that meant women.
